# The robot

The `.core` file declares one robot: a chassis, and the parts placed on it.

```robotdsl
Robot diff_bot {
    intent "Two-wheel differential base with a rear caster and a top lidar"

    Diff_two_caster chassis(ref = "diff_base")
    Standard wheel_l(ref = "standard_80", glue = (0, 0.12, -0.02, 0, 1, 0))
    Standard wheel_r(ref = "standard_80", glue = (0, -0.12, -0.02, 0, -1, 0))
    Caster ball(ref = "caster_ball", glue = (-0.15, 0, -0.035, 0, 0, -1))
    Lidar top_lidar(ref = "lidar_ld06", glue = (0, 0, 0.06, 0, 0, 1))
}
```

Each line is a component: its type, its name, and its arguments. `intent` is an optional sentence for people and for the tools that generate programs.

## The chassis

Exactly one component is the chassis. Its type says how the robot drives, and its `ref` names the chassis part in a library:

```robotdsl
Diff_two_caster chassis(ref = "diff_base")
```

The chassis type decides which wheel mounts must be filled, which of them drive, and what the base can do:

| Chassis type | Wheels | Can spin in place | Holonomic |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Diff_two_caster` | two `Standard`, plus a caster | yes | no |
| `Diff_drive` | four `Standard`, skid steer | yes | no |
| `Tracked` | two `Track`, skid steer | yes | no |
| `Mecanum_four_wheel` | four `Mecanum` | yes | yes |
| `Omni_drive` | four `Omni_wheel` | yes | yes |
| `Omni_three_wheel` | three `Omni_wheel` | yes | yes |
| `Tricycle` | one steered driven front wheel, two free rear wheels | no | no |
| `Ackermann` | two steered front wheels, driven or free, and two driven rear wheels | no | no |
| `Legged` | none: it stands on the feet of its legs, its own links or `Leg` parts placed on it, where their servos hold them | each way its gait turns | to each side its gait moves aside |

A `Legged` chassis is a part with legs of its own, or a body that carries legs: its file names the gait its walking controller takes and, when its legs are its own, the shapes of its links it stands on ([Component library format](../../reference/library.md#feet-and-gait)), and may state that controller, the policy or the gait its legs walk by ([Walking controller](../../reference/library.md#walking-controller)). A body's legs are `Leg` parts, each placed by glue where a hip goes; the chassis's gait walks them all ([Legs as parts](../../reference/library.md#legs-as-parts)), or a walker trained for that body on those legs, placed so, which the library registers, walks it, whatever the body states ([Walkers](../../reference/library.md#walkers)). The `mjcf` target writes a legged base by its controller or its walker; the ROS targets do not write one yet.

[Drive types](../advanced/drive-types.md) says what the compiler emits for each.

## Parts and glue

Every other component is a part placed by `glue`: the point and the direction of a connector, in the chassis frame. The connector is one of the chassis' own, or one of a part already placed: a wheel's glue is the end of its motor's shaft.

```robotdsl
Motor motor_l(ref = "gearmotor_37d", glue = (0, 0.1, -0.02, 0, 1, 0))
Standard wheel_l(ref = "standard_80", glue = (0, 0.12, -0.02, 0, 1, 0))
//                                            x   y     z     nx ny nz
```

The glue must match one connector within 1 mm and 0.01 in direction; one that matches two is an error, and a part that mates onto that part is not placed either. The part's own connector is then mated to it, the two directions facing each other. A seventh number, `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, roll)`, turns the part about the direction.

You do not have to look the values up. A glue that matches no connector is reported with the nearest one and the exact glue to write:

```text
error[validation.assembly.glue_on_connector]: the glue of 'wheel_lf' matches no connector of the chassis or of a placed part; the nearest is 'motor_lf.shaft', 0.008 m away with direction cosine 1.00
   --> demo.core:17:52
   |
17 |     Mecanum wheel_lf(ref = "mecanum_black", glue = (0.12, 0.1494, -0.0216, 0, 1, 0))
   |                                                    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ matches no connector
   |
   = help: to mount on 'motor_lf.shaft' write glue = (0.1275, 0.1494, -0.0216, 0, 1, 0)
   = help: the free connectors are: chassis.front_mount, motor_lf.shaft
```

A connector holds one part. Every mount the chassis type drives carries one wheel of the right type: on the shaft of a `Motor` on the mount, which then bounds the wheel's speed and torque, or straight on the mount, driven within no stated limits when no motor is declared for it (a kit whose motors are built into its chassis). A wheel glued straight onto a mount the type does not drive rolls freely, such as a tricycle's rear wheels. See [Drive types](../advanced/drive-types.md#motors). A `Caster` is passive and may sit on any other connector.

## Power and command

A power or a command connection is not a place, so it is not a glue but a reference to another component. A `MotorDriver` names the `Battery` that feeds it with `power`, and a `Motor` names the driver that drives it with `command`. The battery and the driver are themselves parts glued onto connectors.

```robotdsl
Battery pack(ref = "lipo_3s_2200", glue = (-0.1, 0, 0.0344, 0, 0, -1))
MotorDriver driver(ref = "driver_vnh5019", glue = (0, 0.1, 0.0344, 0, 0, -1), power = @core/pack)
Motor motor_l(ref = "gearmotor_37d", glue = (0, 0.1, -0.02, 0, 1, 0), command = @core/driver)
```

A motor like this one has two terminals, which go to one channel of its driver: the channel that commands it also powers it, so it names no `power`. A motor that carries its driver, a smart servo, is commanded over a bus and powered on a line of its own, and names both: `power = @core/pack, command = @core/board`.

From what the parts state, the compiler then checks that the driver accepts the pack's voltage full and run down, that this voltage includes the one the motor's ratings hold at, that one channel delivers the current the motor draws stalled, and that the driver has a channel, or speaks the bus, for each motor it commands. [Validation](../advanced/validation.md#power-and-command) lists the rules. A program that names no `power` and no `command` still compiles: the rules that would judge them are undecided, without a warning.

## Component types

| Kind | Types |
| --- | --- |
| Motors | `Motor`: on a drive mount, with the wheel it drives on its shaft; `command` names its driver |
| Power | `Battery`: a pack on any free connector. `MotorDriver`: a board on any free connector; `power` names its battery |
| Wheels | `Standard`, `Mecanum`, `Omni_wheel`, `Caster` |
| Legs | `Leg`: a leg of its own, on servos, ending in the feet it stands on, placed on a `Legged` chassis that has no legs of its own |
| Tracks | `Track`: a belt with its sprockets and road wheels as one part, where a `Tracked` chassis has a wheel's place |
| Sensors | `Lidar`, `Lidar3D`, `Camera`, `DepthCamera`, `RGBD`, `IMU`, `Ultrasonic`, `Range`, `Bumper` |
| Other | `Attachment`: an arm, a gripper, a tray; it adds mass and shape, and the compiler does nothing else with it |

A part can be used as a type when its library entry lists that type. The [vocabulary](../../reference/vocabulary.md) lists every type with what it means.

## Names

Component names are how the task and the evaluation refer to parts: `@core/wheel_l`. Two components cannot share a name, and the names of the links the targets add are reserved: `base_footprint`, `base_link`, `<link>_contact_<n>` for a ground contact a part declares, and `<wheel>_steer` for a steered wheel's knuckle.

## Next

[The world](./world.md) places the robot among obstacles and goals.

pages.text:
# The world

The `.world` file declares where the robot starts, what surrounds it, and the places the task refers to.

```robotdsl
World demo {
    physics(gravity = (0, 0, -9.81))
    spawn(robot = @core/diff_bot, pose = (0, 0, 0.05, 0, 0, 0, 1))
    Scenario room(ref = "empty", ground_plane = true) {
        Obstacle box(type = "box", pos = (1.2, 0, 0.25, 0, 0, 0, 1), size = (0.3, 0.3, 0.5))
        Marker flag(type = "cylinder", pos = (2.5, 0, 0.01, 0, 0, 0, 1), size = (0.3, 0.3, 0.02))
    }
    Goal goal(pose = (2.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))
}
```

## Poses

A pose is seven numbers, a position and a quaternion: `(x, y, z, qx, qy, qz, qw)`. No rotation is `(x, y, z, 0, 0, 0, 1)`. Lengths are metres.

## Physics and spawn

`physics(gravity = (x, y, z))` sets gravity in m/s². Without it, the targets use standard gravity, `(0, 0, -9.81)`.

`spawn` places the robot the `.core` file declares:

```robotdsl
spawn(robot = @core/diff_bot, pose = (0, 0, 0.05, 0, 0, 0, 1))
```

## Scenarios and entities

A scenario groups the things in one environment. Its `ref` is the base environment: `"empty"` for none, where the room is whatever the scenario's entities make it, or the id of an environment a library holds, [below](#environments-from-a-library). `ground_plane = true` adds a floor, and without one the robot falls.

Each entity has a type, a name, a shape and a pose:

| Entity type | Is |
| --- | --- |
| `Obstacle` | Something the robot must not touch. Touching one fails the run's physical verdict. |
| `SupportSurface` | A floor, ramp or pad the robot drives on; contact is expected. |
| `Marker` | A visual mark, such as a goal disc. It has no collision unless `collision = true`. |

The shape is a `type` of `"box"`, `"sphere"` or `"cylinder"` with a `size` of `(x, y, z)` in metres; a sphere's diameter and a cylinder's are the `x` size, a cylinder's height the `z` size. Or the entity is an object of a library, named by `ref`, as the next section says.

Entities stay where they are placed. Leave `is_static` out, or write `is_static = true`; an entity declared movable is refused, because an entity states no mass to move it with.

Obstacles are drawn into the navigation map, seen by the robot's sensors, and measured against when a run is judged.

A `Marker` that does not collide is only seen. Both simulators' cameras see it. Gazebo's lasers and range finders see it too, since they see what is shown; MuJoCo's return only from what collides, which `compile.json` says for each such mark.

A program states no light and no colours. Both simulators light a world alike: a sun, a pale sky, a light grey floor, and a mid grey for a shape a program states. A colour camera reads one world in the two within a few parts in 255. A camera draws nothing beyond the far end of its range and shows the sky there: 5 m from it for one that measures depth, 10 m ahead of it for a plain one.

An entity's name is its own, apart from the robot's components. The Gazebo target holds the robot and the floor as models of the same world, so there an entity cannot share the robot's name, or `ground_plane` when the scenario has a floor.

## Objects from a library

A table, a shelf or a ramp is not written as boxes. It is an object of a [component library](./libraries.md#objects-for-the-world), and an entity takes it by its id, as a component takes its part:

```robotdsl
Scenario room(ref = "empty", ground_plane = true) {
    Obstacle table(ref = "work_table", pos = (2.0, 0.6, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))
    SupportSurface ramp(ref = "ramp_10deg", pos = (1.0, -1.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))
    Marker spot(ref = "floor_disc", pos = (3.0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))
}
```

The example library holds a pallet rack, a work table, a pallet jack, a cardboard box, a traffic cone and a pallet, each a model that a collection publishes for simulators, and a ramp and a mark painted on the floor.

The object's library entry states the mesh it is shown by and the shapes it collides by. The program states where it stands, by `pos`, and what it is to the robot, by the entity type: the same crate is an `Obstacle` in one world and a `Marker` in another. A program names no file and no address; where an object's mesh comes from is its library's business.

An entity takes `type` with `size`, or `ref`: never both, and never `size` beside `ref`, since an object is as large as its entry says. An object that declares no collision is only shown, so it can be a `Marker` and cannot be an `Obstacle` or a `SupportSurface`.

The map and the run's verdict take an object by its shapes, each where it stands: a gate by its two posts and not by the passage between them. They take each shape seen from above, as they take a primitive, so a table's top covers the floor under it and a robot is planned around the table, not under it.

Both simulators show an object's mesh to their cameras, in its materials' colours and with the pictures laid on them. Gazebo decodes the mesh, and its lasers see it too. MuJoCo decodes no glTF, so the output's own node reads the mesh, while its lasers see the shapes the object collides by; `compile.json` says so for each object. A laser sees a ramp as it sees a wall, so a robot that navigates by a laser does not plan a way up one.

## Environments from a library

A room or a hall is written once, in a [component library](./libraries.md#objects-for-the-world), and a scenario takes it whole by its id:

```robotdsl
Scenario room(ref = "room_6x4") {
    Obstacle box(type = "box", pos = (1.2, 0, 0.25, 0, 0, 0, 1), size = (0.3, 0.3, 0.5))
}
Goal goal(target = @world/dock)
```

The environment brings its floor and its entities: here a storeroom of four walls, with a loaded pallet rack, a work table, a pallet with two cartons, a pallet jack, a traffic cone and a mark on the floor called `dock`. They are the scenario's own beside the ones the program adds: drawn into the map, seen by the sensors, judged against, and named like any entity, so a goal can target the room's `dock` and a task drive to it. An entity the program adds cannot take a name the environment already holds.

An environment that brings its floor needs no `ground_plane`. A world has one floor: `ground_plane = true` is refused as a second where an environment of any of the world's scenarios brings its floor, or where another scenario already lays it. The floors of two environments are that one floor. An environment's entities stand where its library entry places them, in the world's frame; a scenario does not move or turn the environment it takes.

## Goals

A goal is a named place the task can drive to, given by a `pose` or by an entity as `target`:

```robotdsl
Goal goal(pose = (2.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))
Goal at_flag(target = @world/flag)
```

The task refers to it as `@world/goal`.

## Next

[The task](./task.md) says what the robot does in this world.

pages.text:
# The task

The `.task` file is what the robot must do, as a behavior tree: actions such as `Navigate` and `Spin`, arranged by control nodes such as `Sequence` and `Retry`.

```robotdsl
Task drone_demo(timeout_s = 120) {
    Retry(count = 2) {
        Navigate(goal = @world/goal)
    }
    Sequence {
        Spin(angle_rad = 1.57),
        Wait(duration_s = 2),
        Stop()
    }
}
```

The nodes in the task's body run in order. `timeout_s` bounds the whole task; when it runs out, the run ends with status `timeout`.

## Actions

| Action | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `Navigate(goal = @world/...)` | Drive to a goal or an entity, avoiding obstacles |
| `Spin(angle_rad = ...)` | Turn in place by a signed angle |
| `Advance(distance_m = ..., speed_mps = ...)` | Drive straight ahead; the speed is optional |
| `BackUp(distance_m = ..., speed_mps = ...)` | Drive straight back |
| `Strafe(distance_m = ..., speed_mps = ...)` | Drive sideways, positive to the left |
| `Wait(duration_s = ...)` | Do nothing for a while |
| `Stop()` | Come to rest |

An action with no arguments keeps its parentheses, `Stop()`, so two nodes in a row never read as one.

## Control flow

| Node | Runs its children |
| --- | --- |
| `Sequence { ... }` | In order, stopping at the first failure |
| `Fallback { ... }` | In order, stopping at the first success |
| `Parallel(policy = "success_on_all") { ... }` | Together; `"success_on_one"` succeeds when any child does |
| `Retry(count = n) { ... }` | Its one child again until it succeeds, at most `n` times |
| `Repeat(count = n) { ... }` | Its one child `n` times |
| `Timeout(timeout_s = t) { ... }` | Its one child, failing it after `t` seconds |
| `Inverter { ... }` | Its one child, swapping success and failure |

Conditions are leaves that succeed or fail without moving: `GoalReached(goal = ...)`, `DistanceTraveled(distance_m = ...)` and `TimeExpired(duration_s = ...)`.

```robotdsl
Task deliver(timeout_s = 180) {
    Fallback {
        GoalReached(goal = @world/goal),
        Retry(count = 3) {
            Navigate(goal = @world/goal)
        }
    }
    Stop()
}
```

## What, not how

The task names what the robot must accomplish, not how a navigation stack does it. There is no node for a planner, a controller or a costmap, and no syntax to pick one; the target binds each action to its stack. [The output contract](../../reference/output.md#the-task) lists what each action becomes.

The base has to be able to do what the task asks. `Spin` needs a base that turns in place, and `Strafe` a holonomic one; a tricycle asked to spin is an error at compile time, not a surprise in the simulator.

## Next

[The evaluation](./evaluation.md) says how a run of this task is judged.

pages.text:
# The evaluation

The `.eval` file is optional. It lists checks, each a measurement of the run with bounds it must stay within.

```robotdsl
Evaluate demo_eval {
    Check_clearance(target = @world/goal, min = 0.3)
    Check_vel(target = @core/wheel_lf, min = 0, max = 60)
    Check_time(target = @task/drone_demo, max = 300)
}
```

Every check takes a `target` and at least one of `min` and `max`.

## Checks

| Check | Measures | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Check_vel` | A joint's speed, rad/s, every sample | a wheel, `@core/...` |
| `Check_acc` | A joint's acceleration, rad/s², every sample | a wheel |
| `Check_jerk` | A joint's jerk, rad/s³, every sample | a wheel |
| `Check_effort` | A joint's effort, N·m, every sample | a wheel |
| `Check_distance` | Distance to a goal or entity: `min` bounds the closest approach, `max` the distance at the end | `@world/...` |
| `Check_clearance` | The closest approach to an obstacle over the run | `@world/...`, or every obstacle |
| `Check_contact` | Seconds a part spends touching a scene entity | a part, `@core/...` |
| `Check_time` | The task's duration, seconds | `@task/...` |

`Check_distance` and `Check_clearance` also take a `source`, the part measured from; without it they measure from the whole robot. On a `Bumper`, `Check_contact` reads what the bumper itself reported; on any other part, the simulator's geometry.

## How checks are judged

A check is judged from the simulator's own record of the run, never from what the robot or its navigation stack believed: the robot's pose as the simulator publishes it, the joint states, and the bumpers' reports. Each check ends `pass`, `fail` or `unknown`. A check with no samples to judge is `unknown`, never `pass`.

A joint check on a part that has no moving joint is refused at compile time, since there would be nothing to measure.

The checks are one of three verdicts a run gets; [Judging a run](../advanced/judging-a-run.md) explains the other two.

## Next

[Component libraries](./libraries.md) explains where the parts come from.

pages.text:
# Vocabulary

This page is generated from `mobiledsl.semantic.model.vocabulary`; edit the code,
not the page. It lists every name a program may use beyond the grammar's
keywords, and what each takes. Numbers carry no unit: the parameter name carries
it by suffix (`_s` seconds, `_m` metres, `_rad` radians, `_mps` metres per second).

## Component types (`.core`)

A component type is the kind of part a program places. A part can be used as a
type when its library entry lists the type under `profiles`; the type's category
is the kind of physical thing the part must be, which decides what its entry
declares (a wheel its radius, a chassis its connectors). The chassis takes only
`ref`; every other component is placed by `glue`. A type exists only when the
compiler acts on it: a chassis type has kinematics, a wheel type a contact model,
a track type a belt the targets stand in for, a sensor type a simulated sensor and a
use for its data, a motor ratings that bound its wheel, a battery and a motor driver
ratings the power and command rules judge.
Everything the compiler merely carries is an `Attachment`; the library entry says
what the part is.

| Type | Category | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Mecanum_four_wheel` | chassis | Four mecanum wheels; holonomic. |
| `Diff_drive` | chassis | Four driven standard wheels, skid steer. |
| `Diff_two_caster` | chassis | Two driven standard wheels and a caster. |
| `Tricycle` | chassis | One steered, driven front wheel and two free rear wheels. |
| `Ackermann` | chassis | Two steered front wheels, two driven rear wheels; the front wheels may be driven too. |
| `Omni_drive` | chassis | Four omni wheels; holonomic. |
| `Omni_three_wheel` | chassis | Three omni wheels on a circle; holonomic. |
| `Tracked` | chassis | Two tracks, each driven on its own; skid steer. |
| `Legged` | chassis | Legs on servos, its own or Leg parts placed on it; stands on their feet, walks as its gait states. |
| `Mecanum` | wheel | A mecanum wheel. |
| `Standard` | wheel | A plain driven wheel. |
| `Caster` | wheel | A passive support wheel. |
| `Omni_wheel` | wheel | An omni wheel. |
| `Track` | track | A track as one part: a belt around its sprockets and road wheels. It mates by the hub that drives it and moves the base by the travel its part states per turn. |
| `Motor` | motor | A motor on a drive mount of the chassis, where the wheel glued onto its shaft is driven, or on a seat of the chassis whose driveline turns the wheels of other mounts; within the speed and torque its part states. Its `command` names the motor driver that drives it. |
| `Battery` | battery | A battery pack, placed by its glue as any part is; the parts whose `power` names it run on the voltage its part states. |
| `MotorDriver` | motor_driver | A board that drives motors: each motor without a bus from a channel of its own, within the current its part states, and motors that carry their driver over a bus it speaks. |
| `Lidar` | sensor | A planar laser scanner. |
| `Lidar3D` | sensor | A spinning multi-ring laser; its cloud marks obstacles and its middle ring can stand in for a planar laser. |
| `Camera` | sensor | An RGB camera. |
| `DepthCamera` | sensor | A depth camera; its cloud can stand in for a laser. |
| `RGBD` | sensor | A colour camera with a registered depth image; its cloud can stand in for a laser. |
| `IMU` | sensor | An inertial measurement unit. |
| `Ultrasonic` | sensor | A range finder that measures with sound in a narrow cone; its reading marks the costmaps' range layer. |
| `Range` | sensor | A range finder that measures with light (infrared or time of flight) in a narrow cone; its part states its range, cone and rate, and its reading marks the costmaps' range layer. |
| `Bumper` | sensor | A contact switch on the body; Check_contact on it reads what pressed it. |
| `Attachment` | attachment | A part the compiler carries but does not act on: an arm, a gripper, a tray. It adds mass and shape; the library entry says what it is. |
| `Leg` | leg | A leg of a Legged chassis that has none of its own: links on hinges its servos turn, ending in the feet it stands on; the chassis's gait walks it with the others. |

Parameters of a chassis:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | string | yes | The library part id. |

Parameters of a wheel, track, sensor, battery, or attachment:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | string | yes | The library part id. |
| `glue` | tuple of 6 or 7 | yes | Where the part mates: a connector of the chassis or of a part already placed, `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz)` or with a roll angle `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, roll)`. The point and the unit normal are in the chassis frame; the part's connector is aligned to them. |

Parameters of a motor:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | string | yes | The library part id. |
| `glue` | tuple of 6 or 7 | yes | Where the part mates: a connector of the chassis or of a part already placed, `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz)` or with a roll angle `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, roll)`. The point and the unit normal are in the chassis frame; the part's connector is aligned to them. |
| `power` | `@core/<battery or motor driver>` | no | What the motor draws its power from. A motor without a bus is powered through the driver that commands it and needs no `power` beside `command`; one with a bus names its supply here. |
| `command` | `@core/<motor driver>` | no | The motor driver that commands the motor: from one of its channels, or over the motor's bus. |

Parameters of a motor driver:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | string | yes | The library part id. |
| `glue` | tuple of 6 or 7 | yes | Where the part mates: a connector of the chassis or of a part already placed, `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz)` or with a roll angle `(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, roll)`. The point and the unit normal are in the chassis frame; the part's connector is aligned to them. |
| `power` | `@core/<battery>` | no | The battery the driver is fed by. |

### Chassis types

What each chassis type needs and what the assembled base can do. A mount is
driven in one of three ways. A `Motor` sits on it, its `glue` equal to the chassis
connector that the part's profile maps the mount to, with one wheel of an allowed
type on the motor's shaft. Or the wheel sits on the mount itself and a `Motor`
sits on a connector of the chassis whose `driveline` turns that mount. Or the wheel
sits on a mount the type always drives and no motor is declared: the kit's motors
are then part of its chassis, and the targets drive the wheel within no stated
limits and say so. On a mount that does not drive, or on an optional mount with
no motor, the wheel sits alone and rolls freely. A `Caster` wheel is
passive and may sit on any other connector. Every mount is driven unless the
table lists the driven ones; a mount listed as optional is driven or free, together
with the others listed so. One motor turns one mount, or through a driveline one
of the sets under shared drive. A mount that steers turns about the kingpin the
chassis part declares on that connector. A `Tracked` base carries a `Track` where
the others carry a wheel, on its two mounts, and they are driven the same two ways.
A `Legged` base carries neither: its legs are its part's own links, or `Leg` parts
placed on it when it has none of its own. It stands on their feet, where their servos
hold them, and its part's `gait` says what its walking controller takes: it moves
aside when the gait takes a speed aside, and turns in place when the gait takes a turn.

| Chassis | Wheel mounts | Wheel type | Driven | Shared drive | Steered | Holonomic | Spins in place |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Mecanum_four_wheel` | `front_left_wheel`, `front_right_wheel`, `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel` | `Mecanum` | all | none | none | yes | yes |
| `Diff_drive` | `front_left_wheel`, `front_right_wheel`, `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel` | `Standard` | all | `front_left_wheel` + `rear_left_wheel`; `front_right_wheel` + `rear_right_wheel` | none | no | yes |
| `Diff_two_caster` | `left_wheel`, `right_wheel` | `Standard` | all | none | none | no | yes |
| `Tricycle` | `front_wheel`, `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel` | `Standard` | `front_wheel` | none | `front_wheel` | no | no |
| `Ackermann` | `front_left_wheel`, `front_right_wheel`, `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel` | `Standard` | `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel`; optional: `front_left_wheel`, `front_right_wheel` | `rear_left_wheel` + `rear_right_wheel`; `front_left_wheel` + `front_right_wheel`; `front_left_wheel` + `front_right_wheel` + `rear_left_wheel` + `rear_right_wheel` | `front_left_wheel`, `front_right_wheel` | no | no |
| `Omni_drive` | `front_left_wheel`, `front_right_wheel`, `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel` | `Omni_wheel` | all | none | none | yes | yes |
| `Omni_three_wheel` | `front_wheel`, `rear_left_wheel`, `rear_right_wheel` | `Omni_wheel` | all | none | none | yes | yes |
| `Tracked` | `left_track`, `right_track` | `Track` | all | none | none | no | yes |
| `Legged` | none: it stands on its feet | none | none | none | none | its gait's | its gait's |

## World (`.world`)

### Entity types

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Obstacle` | Something the robot must not touch: touching it fails the run. |
| `SupportSurface` | A floor, ramp or pad the robot drives on; contact is expected. |
| `Marker` | A visual mark such as a line or a goal disc; no collision by default. |

All entity types take the same parameters:

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `type` | `box`, `sphere`, `cylinder` | no | A primitive shape; exactly one of `type` and `ref`. |
| `ref` | string | no | The id of a library object, shown by its mesh and colliding by the shapes its entry declares; exactly one of `type` and `ref`. |
| `pos` | tuple of 7 | yes | World pose `(x, y, z, qx, qy, qz, qw)`; no rotation is `(x, y, z, 0, 0, 0, 1)`. |
| `size` | tuple of 3 | no | Primitive dimensions `(x, y, z)` in metres; required with `type`, refused with `ref`. |
| `is_static` | bool | no | Fixed in place (default `true`). No target moves an entity: it states no mass to move it with, so `false` is refused. |
| `collision` | bool | no | Emits collision geometry (default depends on the type). An object that declares no collision cannot collide. |

### `Scenario`

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | string | yes | The base environment: the id of a library environment, whose floor and entities the scenario takes, or `empty` for none. |
| `ground_plane` | bool | no | Lay the world's ground plane (default `false`). A world has one: this is refused where an environment of any of its scenarios brings its floor, or another scenario already lays it. |

### `Goal`

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pose` | tuple of 7 | no | The goal pose `(x, y, z, qx, qy, qz, qw)`; one of `pose` and `target`. |
| `target` | `@world/<entity>` | no | An entity whose pose is the goal; one of `pose` and `target`. |

### `physics`

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gravity` | tuple of 3 | no | Gravity `(x, y, z)` in m/s^2. |

### `spawn`

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `robot` | `@core/<robot>` | yes | The robot declared in the `.core` file. |
| `pose` | tuple of 7 | yes | Where the robot starts, `(x, y, z, qx, qy, qz, qw)`. |

## Task (`.task`)

### `Task`

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `timeout_s` | number | no | The whole task must finish within this many seconds. |

### Composites (take children)

#### `Sequence`

Run children in order; stop at the first failure.

No parameters.

#### `Fallback`

Run children in order; stop at the first success.

No parameters.

#### `Parallel`

Run children together.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `policy` | `success_on_all`, `success_on_one` | yes | When the parallel succeeds. |

### Decorators (take exactly one child)

#### `Retry`

Re-run the child until it succeeds, at most `count` times.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `count` | number | yes | Number of attempts. |

#### `Repeat`

Run the child `count` times.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `count` | number | yes | Number of attempts. |

#### `Timeout`

Fail the child if it runs longer than `timeout_s`.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `timeout_s` | number | yes | Seconds. |

#### `Inverter`

Swap the child's success and failure.

No parameters.

### Actions

#### `Navigate`

Drive to a goal, avoiding obstacles.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `goal` | `@world/<goal or entity>` | yes | A goal or an entity in the world. |

#### `Wait`

Do nothing for a while.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `duration_s` | number | yes | Seconds. |

#### `Stop`

Come to rest.

No parameters.

#### `Spin`

Turn in place.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `angle_rad` | number | yes | Signed angle in radians. |

#### `Advance`

Drive straight ahead.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `distance_m` | number | yes | Distance in metres. |
| `speed_mps` | number | no | Speed in m/s. |

#### `BackUp`

Drive straight back.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `distance_m` | number | yes | Distance in metres. |
| `speed_mps` | number | no | Speed in m/s. |

#### `Strafe`

Drive sideways; needs a holonomic base.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `distance_m` | number | yes | Signed distance in metres; positive is left. |
| `speed_mps` | number | no | Speed in m/s. |

### Conditions

#### `GoalReached`

True when the robot is at the goal.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `goal` | `@world/<goal or entity>` | yes | A goal or an entity in the world. |

#### `DistanceTraveled`

True once the robot has moved this far.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `distance_m` | number | yes | Distance in metres. |

#### `TimeExpired`

True once this much time has passed.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `duration_s` | number | yes | Seconds. |

## Evaluate (`.eval`)

### `Check_vel`

Joint speed in rad/s: the magnitude of every sample stays within the bounds.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@core/<component>` | yes | The wheel or joint to observe. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_acc`

Joint acceleration in rad/s^2, the difference of successive speed samples; every sample stays within the bounds.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@core/<component>` | yes | The wheel or joint to observe. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_jerk`

Joint jerk in rad/s^3, the second difference of the speed samples; every sample stays within the bounds.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@core/<component>` | yes | The wheel or joint to observe. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_effort`

Joint effort in N*m: the magnitude of every sample stays within the bounds.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@core/<component>` | yes | The wheel or joint to observe. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_distance`

Distance in metres from the robot (or `source`) to `target`: `min` bounds the closest approach over the run, `max` the distance when the task ends. The robot is measured from its recorded position, a part from a point of its own shape seen from above, its declared ground contacts aside: the middle of the rectangle around its box or hull, square to the chassis; the centre of a wheel; the middle of a track's run on the ground where the track declares no shape; the part's origin where it declares no collision.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@world/<goal or entity>` | yes | The entity or goal measured to. |
| `source` | `@core/<component>` | no | The robot part measured from. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_clearance`

Distance in metres from the robot (or `source`) to the nearest obstacle, at its closest over the run.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@world/<goal or entity>` | no | The obstacle to measure to; every obstacle when absent or not an obstacle. |
| `source` | `@core/<component>` | no | The robot part measured from. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_contact`

Seconds the robot part `target` spends touching a scene entity: what its contact switch reports when it is a Bumper, else the simulator's geometry.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@core/<component>` | yes | The robot part. |
| `source` | `@core/<component>` | no | The robot part measured from. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

### `Check_time`

Duration of the task in seconds, from its first tick to its last.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | `@task/<task>` | yes | The task. |
| `min` | number | no | Lower bound; at least one bound is required. |
| `max` | number | no | Upper bound; at least one bound is required. |

# Grammar

A program is four files: the robot (`.core`), the world (`.world`), the task
(`.task`), and optionally the evaluation (`.eval`). Each file holds exactly one
declaration of its kind. The files are given to the compiler on the command
line, and the extension says which form a file is. There is no project
manifest: the target, the component libraries, and the output directory are
compile-time settings, so they are command-line options, not something the
author writes next to the program.

The grammar fixes the statement forms and nothing else. Component types, world
entity types, task node types, and check names are ordinary names that later
phases resolve against the standard vocabulary, the component libraries, and
the target. A file that names a component or an action the compiler has never
seen is syntactically valid; whether the name exists is decided by name
resolution, not here. Adding vocabulary never changes the grammar.

The normative grammar is `src/mobiledsl/frontend/grammar/robotdsl.lark`, read
by Lark with the LALR algorithm and a contextual lexer. The test suite builds
every start rule in strict mode, so no two terminals can match the same text.
When this page and the file disagree, the file is right and this page has a
bug.

## Common forms

Every declaration is a keyword, a name, and a braced body. Inside a body,
items have one of two shapes:

```text
Type name(parameter = value, ...)          a named item of some type
keyword(parameter = value, ...)            a setting with no name
```

Arguments are always named. Items may be separated by commas, by line breaks,
or by both, and a trailing comma is allowed. Comments are `//` to end of line
and `/* ... */`; block comments do not nest. Line endings may be LF or CRLF.

### Values

| Value | Form | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| string | double quotes, JSON escapes | `"mecanum_black"`, `"a \"quoted\" word"` |
| number | optional sign, decimal, optional exponent | `2`, `-0.0216`, `1.5e-1` |
| boolean | `true`, `false` | `is_static = true` |
| tuple | two or more numbers in parentheses | `(0, 0, -9.81)`, `(2.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1)` |
| reference | `@namespace/name` | `@core/wheel_lf`, `@world/goal`, `@task/drone_demo` |

Numbers carry no unit; the parameter name does, by suffix: `timeout_s`,
`distance_m`, `angle_rad`. A tuple's meaning (a pose of seven numbers, a size
of three, a glue of six or seven) is decided by the parameter that takes it,
not by the grammar. The reference namespaces are `core`, `world`, and `task`;
any other namespace is a diagnostic, but the tree is still built. Identifiers
are `[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*`.

## CoreDSL (`.core`)

```text
robot_decl: "Robot" NAME "{" intent? component* "}"
intent:     "intent" STRING
component:  NAME NAME params
```

The first name of a component is its type, the second its instance name.
`intent` is a sentence for people and for the tools that generate programs; it
comes before the components.

```text
Robot drone_mecanum {
    intent "Drone mecanum mobile base with four black mecanum wheels and a top lidar"

    Mecanum_four_wheel chassis(ref = "tslot_1515_drone")
    Mecanum wheel_lf(ref = "mecanum_black", glue = (0.1275, 0.1494, -0.0216, 0, 1, 0))
    Lidar top_lidar(ref = "lidar_ld06", glue = (0, 0.0001, 0.0344, 0, 0, -1))
}
```

## WorldDSL (`.world`)

```text
world_decl: "World" NAME "{" world_item* "}"
world_item: physics | spawn | scenario | goal
physics:    "physics" params
spawn:      "spawn" params
scenario:   "Scenario" NAME params "{" entity* "}"
entity:     NAME NAME params
goal:       "Goal" NAME params
```

`physics` and `spawn` are settings of the world and have no name. A scenario
groups the entities of one environment; each entity has a type (for example
`Obstacle`, `SupportSurface`, `Marker`) and a name that tasks and checks refer
to as `@world/<name>`. A goal is a named location.

```text
World demo {
    physics(gravity = (0, 0, -9.81))
    spawn(robot = @core/drone_mecanum, pose = (0, 0, 0.05, 0, 0, 0, 1))
    Scenario room(ref = "empty", ground_plane = true) {
        Obstacle box(type = "box", pos = (1.2, 0, 0.25, 0, 0, 0, 1), size = (0.3, 0.3, 0.5), is_static = true)
    }
    Goal goal(pose = (2.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1))
}
```

## TaskDSL (`.task`)

```text
task_decl: "Task" NAME params? "{" node* "}"
node:      NAME params block?
         | NAME block
block:     "{" node* "}"
```

A node is a type followed by arguments, a block of children, or both. Which
types take children (`Sequence`, `Fallback`, `Retry`, ...) and which are
actions (`Navigate`, `Spin`, `Wait`, ...) is vocabulary, not grammar. A leaf
keeps its parentheses even when it has no arguments, `Stop()`, so that two
nodes in a row never read as one.

The task vocabulary names what the robot must accomplish. It does not name
how a target accomplishes it: there is no node for a navigation stack's
planner, controller, or costmap, and no syntax to select one. Those choices
belong to the target and its configuration.

```text
Task drone_demo(timeout_s = 120) {
    Retry(count = 2) {
        Navigate(goal = @world/goal)
    }
    Sequence {
        Spin(angle_rad = 1.57),
        Wait(duration_s = 2),
        Stop()
    }
}
```

## EvaluateDSL (`.eval`)

```text
eval_decl: "Evaluate" NAME "{" check* "}"
check:     NAME params
```

```text
Evaluate demo_eval {
    Check_clearance(target = @world/goal, min = 0.3)
    Check_vel(target = @core/wheel_lf, min = 0, max = 60)
    Check_time(target = @task/drone_demo, max = 300)
}
```

## Accepted and rejected

Accepted:

| Source | Why it is interesting |
| --- | --- |
| `Robot r {}` | the smallest declaration of each kind is valid |
| `Robot r { Hovercraft body(ref = "x") }` | unknown vocabulary is a name-resolution question |
| `Task t { Dock(station = @world/dock) }` | so are actions the compiler has never seen |
| `Robot r { A a(ref = "1"), B b(ref = "2"), }` | commas are optional, a trailing one is fine |
| `Task t { Sequence { } Stop() Retry(count = 2) { Stop() } }` | block only, arguments only, both |
| `Task t { Spin(angle_rad = -1.5e-1) }` | signs and exponents |
| `// line` `/* block */` | both comment styles |

Rejected, with the diagnostic it produces:

| Source | Diagnostic |
| --- | --- |
| `World w {}` in a `.core` file | `syntax.unexpected_token`: unexpected 'World'; expected 'Robot' |
| `Robot a {} Robot b {}` | `syntax.unexpected_token`: unexpected 'Robot'; expected end of file |
| `Lidar l("lidar_ld06")` | `syntax.unexpected_token`: expected one of ')', a name — arguments are named |
| `Stop Wait(duration_s = 1)` | `syntax.unexpected_token`: unexpected 'Wait'; expected one of '(', '{' |
| `Goal g(pose = (1))` | `syntax.unexpected_token`: unexpected ')'; expected ',' — a tuple has two or more numbers |
| `Robot r {} # comment` | `syntax.unexpected_character`: `#` comments are gone |
| `/* a /* b */ c */` | `syntax.unexpected_token` at `c` — block comments do not nest |
| `Robot r {` | `syntax.unexpected_eof`: expected one of 'intent', '}', a name |
| `Navigate(goal = @wrold/goal)` | `syntax.unknown_reference_namespace` |
| `Lidar l(ref = "a", ref = "b")` | `syntax.duplicate_parameter`, pointing at both occurrences |

The diagnostics are specified in [Diagnostics](diagnostics.md).

## Changes from the previous compiler

The previous compiler's four grammars are the starting point. What changed,
and why:

- Component types, task node types, and check names were grammar keywords
  (21, 15, and 9 of them). They are names now, so a new sensor, action, or
  check is a vocabulary entry, not a grammar change, and the task language is
  no longer tied to one navigation stack's node set.
- Poses, vectors, and references were strings: `glue="0.1275 0.1494 ..."`,
  `goal="@world/goal"`. They are tuples and references now, so the parser
  checks them and every number has its own span.
- `spawn { "@core/x": "pose" }` is `spawn(robot = @core/x, pose = (...))`, and
  `physics { gravity="..." }` is `physics(gravity = (...))`, the same shape as
  every other setting.
- `ComputePathToPose`, `FollowPath`, `path="{path}"`, `ClearLocalCostmap`,
  `ClearGlobalCostmap`, `controller=`, `planner=`, `PipelineSequence`, and
  `TransformAvailable` are gone from the task language: they described the
  navigation stack, not the task.
- `tick_rate_hz` on `Task` is gone: the previous compiler accepted it and
  never used it.
- `#` comments are gone; `/* */` comments are new.

## What the grammar leaves to later phases

- Whether a name exists and what it is.
- Which parameters a type takes, their types, units, and tuple lengths.
- Whether a reference resolves, and whether its namespace fits the parameter.
- Which node types take children, and whether a task or a robot is complete.
- Whether the target supports an action.
