# Component library format

A component library is a directory the compiler is given with `--library`. It
holds the physical parts a program assembles a robot from, the objects a
world places and the environments a scenario takes. The compiler reads
two kinds of file from it, `library.yaml` and each part's `component.yaml`,
and checks that the assets they name exist. It never opens a mesh, and it
never reads the catalog, archive, or generated pages that a library
repository may keep beside them. There is no install step and no default
location.

This page is the schema. The library repository documents how parts are
built; the compiler is the only implementation of what a declaration means.

## Layout

```text
<library>/
├── library.yaml                     name and the registered ids: parts, objects, environments, walkers
├── parts/<part-id>/
│   ├── component.yaml               the declaration specified here
│   ├── assets/                      the mesh the declaration names, and what that mesh keeps beside it
│   └── ...                          README, LICENSE, CHANGELOG, images, source: not read
└── walkers/<walker-id>/
    ├── walker.yaml                  a walker's declaration (see Walkers)
    └── assets/                      its policy
```

### `library.yaml`

```yaml
name: demo_parts          # an identifier
parts:                    # each id is parts/<id>/component.yaml
  - tslot_1515_drone
  - mecanum_black
walkers:                  # optional; each id is walkers/<id>/walker.yaml
  - quad_walker
```

A part that is not listed does not exist to the compiler. An id listed twice
or without a declaration is a diagnostic; the other parts still load. An
[object](#objects) and an [environment](#environments) are listed and laid out
as a part is; its `category` says which an entry is, so an id names one thing.
A [walker](#walkers) is listed under `walkers` and laid out in `walkers/`.

## `component.yaml`

Values are YAML, read as JSON: only `true` and `false` are booleans, `null`,
`~` and an empty value are null, and a plain scalar is a number when it spells a JSON number
(`1e-3` is a number here, unlike in YAML 1.1). A key given twice is a
diagnostic. A key the schema does not list is a diagnostic; there are no
free-form fields, except inside `provenance`, where unknown keys are ignored.

Every length is in metres, every angle in radians, every mass in kilograms,
and every vector is `[x, y, z]` in the part's own frame: `+X` forward, `+Y`
left, `+Z` up. Every number is 0 or between 1e-100 and 1e30 in size, judged as
the float it reads as: no quantity of a part is smaller or larger, and what
the targets work out from such a number can overflow or be lost to zero. A
zero that a computation left a rounding off, such as -2.7e-32, is within it; a
number written nearer zero than any float, such as 1e-400, reads as 0 but is
no zero, and is not. Nothing is defaulted. A value the declaration does not
state is absent, and a later phase that needs it reports what is missing
rather than assuming.

```yaml
schema_version: 1
id: mecanum_black                    # equals the directory name
category: wheel                      # what the part is; see Fields
description: Black 97 mm mecanum wheel.

visual:                              # the mesh that is shown
  file: assets/model.dae             # relative to the part directory
  xyz: [-0.0002, 0, -0.001]          # where the mesh sits in the part frame
  rpy: [0, 0, 1.57079]

wheel:                               # wheels only, and required for them
  radius: 0.0487                     # across the axle
  width: 0.0479                      # along the axle

inertial:
  mass: 0.09643
  origin_xyz: [0, 0, 0]              # centre of mass
  inertia: {ixx: 7.5613e-05, ixy: 0, ixz: 0, iyy: 7.5613e-05, iyz: 0, izz: 0.000114351}
  source: estimated                  # measured | datasheet | cad_measured | estimated | placeholder
  basis: solid cylinder at 270 kg/m^3   # how an estimate was chosen; required for estimated and placeholder

connectors:                          # mating points, at least one
  mount:
    pos: [-0.0013, 0.0011, 0]
    dir: [0, 0, 1]                   # mating axis, unit length
    joint: {type: continuous, axis: [0, 0, 1]}   # the joint created when mated; fixed when absent

profiles:                            # the component types the part can be used as
  Mecanum:
    mounts: {default: mount}         # logical mount name -> connector
```

### Fields

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | yes | `1` |
| `id` | yes | The part id; must equal the directory name |
| `category` | yes | `chassis`, `wheel`, `track`, `sensor`, `attachment`, `leg`, `motor`, `battery`, or `motor_driver` for a part of a robot; `object` for a thing a world places and `environment` for a place a scenario takes, which state the fields under [Objects](#objects) and [Environments](#environments) and not these |
| `description` | yes | One sentence for people |
| `visual` | yes | `file`, `xyz`, `rpy`. `file` is a relative path to a mesh that exists, in a directory of its own inside the part directory, conventionally `assets/`, and not beside the declaration. That directory goes into an output whole: a mesh may keep what it is made of in other files, a glTF its buffers and textures, an OBJ its materials, and names them by relative path, and the compiler opens no mesh to learn which. So what a mesh names lies in that directory or below it, and nothing else is kept there; each of those files is the part's own, not a link out of the part directory |
| `collision` | no; not for wheels | `type: box` with `size` (three positive numbers) and `origin_xyz`, or `type: hull` with `vertices` (at least four `[x, y, z]` points) and `faces` (triangles as three indices into the vertices, wound either way) that bound a convex solid: a corner more than 1 µm outside a face's plane is refused, and so are triangles that do not close one solid of some volume, every edge bordering exactly two of them and none naming a corner twice or given twice. Stands in for the mesh in collision checks and in the simulators, where a hull is written as a binary STL. Without it the mesh is the collision shape |
| `wheel` | wheels only, required | `radius`, `width`, both positive. A wheel's rolling contact is derived from these, so a wheel declares no `collision` |
| `track` | a `Track` part, required; no other part | A track's belt, from its maker's data: `travel_per_turn_m`, how far the belt travels per turn of the hub the part mates by (positive), when the maker's data gives it; `width` (positive); and `ground: {from: [x, y, z], to: [x, y, z]}`, the two ends of the belt's run on the ground in the part frame, which may not be one point. The travel is stated and not a radius: a link tread moves its sprocket's teeth times its links' pitch per turn, less than the sprocket's outline gives. Without it `kinematics.tracks_state_their_travel` cannot decide and no target drives the base. A track may declare a `collision` box around its whole unit, for the footprint; in the simulators it collides through a box on its belt's run |
| `inertial` | yes | `mass` (positive), `origin_xyz`, `inertia` (all six terms; `ixx`, `iyy`, `izz` positive, and the principal moments, which the products `ixy`, `ixz`, `iyz` turn the diagonal into, positive and each at most the sum of the other two, judged in exact arithmetic on the numbers as stated, allowing for their rounding to the nearest doubles, 5 × 2⁻⁵³ of the largest entry: a thin plate stated in round decimals on the edge passes, and a tensor beyond it by more does not; a part's own tensor, which the MuJoCo targets hand on as it is stated, is held as MuJoCo holds it too, its two lesser principal moments adding up in floats to at least the largest, and a link's, which the `mjcf` target writes within the inequality, is not), `source`, `basis` |
| `connectors` | yes, non-empty | Named mating points, below |
| `profiles` | yes | The component types the part can be used as, below. A part with `profiles: {}` is a catalog entry that no program can select |
| `motor` | a `Motor` part, required; no other part | What the motor's datasheet states: `rated_voltage_v`, the voltage its ratings hold at, and at that voltage `no_load_speed_rad_s`, `stall_torque_nm` and `stall_current_a` (its output shaft's speed unloaded, its torque stalled and the current it then draws), all positive. The wheel on its shaft turns within that speed and torque. `voltage_min_v` and `voltage_max_v`, the supply it accepts, only when its maker states them: both or neither, the minimum not negative, the rated voltage between them. `bus`, a name, when the motor carries its driver and is commanded over that bus |
| `battery` | a `Battery` part, required; no other part | What the battery's page states: `voltage_nominal_v`, the voltage it is sold by (positive); `voltage_min_v` and `voltage_max_v`, what it delivers run down and full, both or neither, both positive and the nominal between them; `capacity_ah` (positive) when stated. A pack that states no range leaves the voltage rules undecided |
| `driver` | a `MotorDriver` part, required; no other part | What the board's datasheet states. `channels`, a positive integer: the motors it drives from outputs of its own; with it, required, `voltage_min_v` and `voltage_max_v` (the motor supply it accepts, the minimum not negative) and `continuous_current_per_channel_a`, and `peak_current_per_channel_a` when stated, not below the continuous. `buses`, a list of names: the buses it commands motors over that carry their driver. A board states `channels`, `buses`, or both; one with `buses` alone may state its supply range. `output_voltage_v` when it regulates what it feeds its motors and does not pass its supply on |
| `range` | a `Range` part, required; an `Ultrasonic` part, optional; no other part | What a range finder measures, from its datasheet: `min_m` (not negative), `max_m` (positive, at least `min_m`), `field_of_view_rad` (the full cone about `+x`, positive and below pi) and `rate_hz` (positive). Equal `min_m` and `max_m` make a fixed-distance sensor, which says only whether something is within that distance. The part's frame is the sensor's emitter: its origin where the beam starts, `+x` along it |
| `contacts` | no | A list of `{xyz, radius, note}`: molded ground contacts of a chassis, such as a skid or a ball, as spheres. The statics rule counts each one that reaches the wheels' plane, and the targets simulate each as a sphere that slides |
| `links` | a leg's, required; a chassis's or an attachment's, optional; no other part's | The bodies the part moves below its frame, [below](#links) |
| `provenance` | no | `name`, `manufacturer`, `source_url`, `license`; each a string or `null`. `license` is an SPDX expression when known. Any other key here is ignored: a library may keep what its own tools need (a price, a maker's catalog number) with the part, and the compiler never sees it |

### Connectors

A connector is where another part mates. `pos` is the mating point, `dir`
the mating axis: a wheel's axle, a mount's normal. Two parts mate with their
`dir` vectors anti-parallel and their `pos` points coincident. `up`, when
given, fixes the roll about `dir` for a part whose orientation matters (a
camera lens, a lidar scan plane, a deck); it must be a unit vector
perpendicular to `dir`. A rotation-symmetric part states no `up`.

`joint` is the joint that mating this connector creates: `{type: fixed}` (the
default), or `continuous`, `revolute`, or `prismatic` with a unit `axis`. A
wheel's axle connector carries `continuous`; a chassis mount carries nothing.
Only a wheel turns on its connector. The targets refuse a moving joint on a
connector a mating uses (`target.unsupported`): on the mating part's own
connector unless the part is a wheel, and on the connector it mates onto
whatever mates there. A connector no mating uses is not checked. A chassis, an
attachment or a leg moves bodies of its own through `links`.

`well`, when given, is the void inside the part's collision box that what mates on
this connector may fill: `{radius: 0.052, width: 0.084}` is a cylinder about the
connector's axis, centred on it. A box is a bound drawn around the whole part, so a
kit's chassis box covers the arches its wheels turn in and a motor's box the hub its
wheel sits against; the clearance rules let a part into the declared shape exactly as
far as a well on the connector it mates by, or mates onto, holds, and no further.

`steering` is stated by a chassis on a wheel mount that steers:
`{axis: [0, 0, 1], max_angle_rad: 0.6}` is the kingpin's axis in the part
frame and how far the wheel turns each way. Only a chassis may state it, and
the connector of every mount its chassis type steers must. The compiler
articulates the kingpin; the steering actuator and the knuckle body are the
target's.

`driveline` is stated by a chassis on a connector where a motor seats to turn
wheels that sit on other connectors, through shafts and gears of the chassis'
own: `{turns: [hub_rear_left, hub_rear_right], reduction: 2.33}` names the
connectors whose wheels the motor turns, and how many turns of the motor's
shaft make one turn of theirs. A car's axle with one motor and a differential
is the case. `reduction` is stated when the maker's data gives it; without it
the targets leave those wheels' joints without limits and say so. Only a
chassis may state a driveline, each connector it names once, and none of them
a connector that states a driveline itself. Which wheels one motor may turn
together is vocabulary, as is which mounts drive.

### Links

A chassis, an attachment or a leg may move bodies of its own below its frame:
a legged robot's legs, a pan-tilt mount's head, a leg's thigh and shin. `links`
maps each
link's name, an identifier, to what it states, each link after the one it
hangs from:

```yaml
links:
  head:
    parent: null                     # the part frame, or a link declared above this one
    joint: {type: revolute, xyz: [0, 0, 0.02], rpy: [0, 0, 0], axis: [0, 0, 1], range: [-1.57, 1.57]}
    inertial:
      mass: 0.04
      origin_xyz: [0, 0, 0.015]
      inertia: {ixx: 1.1e-05, ixy: 0, ixz: 0, iyy: 1.1e-05, iyz: 0, izz: 1.0e-05}
      source: estimated
      basis: a 40 g servo of 30 by 50 by 30 mm
    visual: {file: assets/head.glb, xyz: [0, 0, 0], rpy: [0, 0, 0]}
    collision:                       # the shapes it collides by; absent when it touches nothing
      - {type: box, size: [0.03, 0.05, 0.03], origin_xyz: [0, 0, 0.015], rpy: [0, 0, 0]}
    servo: {kp: 4.0, damping: 0.05, armature: 0.0002, frictionloss: 0.01, effort: 0.6, hold: 0.5}
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `parent` | yes | `null` for the part frame, or the name of a link declared above this one |
| `joint` | yes | `type`, `xyz`, `rpy`: the link's frame is its parent's, moved to `xyz` and turned by the fixed-axis roll, pitch and yaw `rpy`. A `revolute` joint then turns it about `axis`, a unit vector in the link's own frame, within `range: [lowest, highest]`, in radians, the lowest below the highest. A `fixed` joint states no `axis` and no `range` |
| `inertial` | yes | As a part's, in the link's frame |
| `visual` | yes | As a part's, in the link's frame |
| `collision` | no | A list of at least one shape, as an object's, in the link's frame, or a `capsule`, a cylinder with half a sphere on each end: its diameter in `x` and in `z` the distance between the centres of its two ends. Without it the link collides with nothing |
| `servo` | a revolute joint's, required; not a fixed one's | The position servo that turns the joint, as a simulator holds it: `kp` (N m/rad, positive), how stiffly it pulls toward the angle it is told; `damping` (N m s/rad), `armature`, the turning inertia of its motor behind its gearbox (kg m²), and `frictionloss` (N m), none negative; `effort` (N m, positive), the most torque it gives; `hold`, within the joint's range, the angle it holds when nothing commands it (rad); and `basis`, when given, where the values come from. Nothing stands in for a value the library does not state |

The part's own `inertial` is its base alone, the body at its frame that the
links hang from: the compiler adds each link's mass to it, so a part whose maker
states the whole product's mass states the base's share of it there and each
link's in that link. The compiler weighs each link and places it where its
servo holds it: the robot's mass and centre of mass, its footprint and the
clearance between its parts take each link there. A sphere and a capsule are
judged for clearance as they are, by the distance from the sphere's centre or
from the segment between the capsule's two centres less the radius; only to
tell whether a well lets one in is it taken as the solid of flat faces drawn
around it, whose corners stand no more than 1.74 % of its radius past it, so that a
well never lets in more than it holds. A part's own links are not judged
against each other or against its base, which they meet at their joints. A well
on a connector lets things only into the part's own declared shape, never into a
link's: a clearance finding names the shape it is of, and for a link advises a
tighter shape, or, when its joint or one it hangs from turns, that joint's servo
holding it elsewhere. The `mjcf` target writes a part's links, each a body on
a hinge its servo turns or fixed to the link above it
([the output reference](output.md#the-mjcf-target));
`ros-gz-nav2` and `ros-mujoco-nav2` do not write them yet, and refuse such a
part (`target.unsupported`).

### Feet and gait

A chassis used as `Legged` walks on legs: its own links, or legs that are
parts of their own placed on it ([Legs as parts](#legs-as-parts)). Its profiles
list `Legged`, with at least one mount, such as a deck others mount on; it states
what its walking controller takes, and, when its legs are its own, its `links`
and the shapes on them it stands on:

```yaml
profiles:
  Legged: {mounts: {deck: deck}}
feet:                                # the shapes on its links that stand on the floor
  front_left: {link: FL_knee, shape: 1, friction: 0.8}
  front_right: {link: FR_knee, shape: 1, friction: 0.8}
gait: {ahead: [-0.5, 1.0], aside: [-0.4, 0.4], turn: [-1.0, 1.0]}
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `feet` | a leg's, and a `Legged` chassis's whose legs are its own, required; no other part's | Each foot by a name, an identifier: the `link` it is on, the `shape` it is among that link's `collision`, counting from 0, a sphere, a capsule or a box, and the `friction` it grips the floor with (positive). Two feet name two shapes |
| `gait` | a `Legged` chassis's, required; no other part's | What its walking controller takes, in the chassis frame: `ahead` and `aside`, its speeds ahead and to its left (m/s), and `turn`, its turn to the left (rad/s), each `[lowest, highest]` with standing still, 0, among them |

The robot stands where the servos hold its legs, each `hold`: the compiler finds
each foot's points lowest down there, below a sphere's centre, below a capsule's
lower end or both ends of one lying flat, a box's lowest corners, each point
within 2 mm of the foot's lowest standing with it, as the feet stand within 2 mm
of one plane; the ground is where they stand. `assembly.feet_touch_the_ground`
asks that every foot stand on the ground with the others, and points at the foot
and at the servos that hold it; `assembly.wheels_touch_one_plane` asks the same of
a wheel or a caster placed under the chassis; and `assembly.links_clear_the_ground`
that no other shape of the links reach below the ground, which finds a foot named
by the wrong shape. The statics rule takes the feet as the robot's supports, and
cannot judge them while one stands off the ground.

The gait says which way and how fast the base goes. A `Spin` needs a turn that
way and a `Strafe` a speed aside to that side, an `Advance` and a `Navigate` a
speed ahead and a `BackUp` one back, and a `speed_mps` the task states may be no
more than the gait's that way (`kinematics.spin_supported`,
`kinematics.strafe_supported` and `kinematics.walk_supported`). A `Navigate`
needs a turn either way, as a navigation planner turns a robot either way to follow its path.
An `Advance`, a `BackUp` or a `Strafe` without a speed is judged by its way
alone: the speed it goes at is the target's.

The feet and the gait are the `Legged` type's, and a leg's feet are its own. A
part whose profiles list another type too stands, used as that type, on that
type's wheels or tracks, its feet being shapes of its links like the rest. A
`Legged` chassis has no wheel or track mounts. The two ROS targets refuse a legged
base for its links, its part's or its legs'; the `mjcf` target writes one that
walks by the walking controller its part states, or by a [walker](#walkers), and
one that walks by neither standing, the model a walker for it is trained on.

#### Legs as parts

A leg may be a part of its own, of category `leg`, used as a `Leg`: a leg made
or sold apart from the body it walks under, placed by glue on a `Legged` chassis
that has no legs of its own. Such a chassis is a body: it states its `gait`, and
no `feet`, and walks by the gait its controller states or by a
[walker](#walkers) trained for it on its legs; links of its own, a head or arms,
are no legs, and a gait holds them where their servos hold them. Each leg states
its `links`, on hinges its servos turn from its frame down, and the `feet` on
them, as a chassis's own legs do, and neither a `gait` nor a `controller`: the
chassis's controller, or its walker, walks all its legs together.

```yaml
# parts/hip_leg/component.yaml, in part
category: leg
connectors:
  mount: {pos: [0, 0, 0], dir: [0, 0, 1], up: [1, 0, 0]}   # where it meets the body
profiles:
  Leg: {mounts: {default: mount}}
links:                               # a thigh on a hip and a shin on a knee, both pitching
  hip:
    parent: null
    joint: {type: revolute, xyz: [0, 0, 0], rpy: [0, 0, 0], axis: [0, 1, 0], range: [-1.5, 1.5]}
    # its inertial, visual, collision and servo, as under Links
  knee:
    parent: hip
    joint: {type: revolute, xyz: [0, 0, -0.15], rpy: [0, 0, 0], axis: [0, 1, 0], range: [-2.6, 0]}
    # the same; its second collision shape is a ball at the shin's end
feet:                                # the ball the leg stands on
  foot: {link: knee, shape: 1, friction: 0.8}
```

```robotdsl
Robot quad {
    Legged body(ref = "quad_body")
    Leg front_left(ref = "hip_leg", glue = (0.12, 0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1))
    Leg front_right(ref = "hip_leg", glue = (0.12, -0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1))
    Leg rear_left(ref = "hip_leg", glue = (-0.12, 0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1))
    Leg rear_right(ref = "hip_leg", glue = (-0.12, -0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1))
}
```

The robot stands on the feet of all its legs, each foot named by its leg in a
finding, and every rule above takes them as it takes a chassis's own.
`assembly.legs_on_a_legged_chassis` asks that every leg be placed on a `Legged`
chassis with no legs of its own, hanging from no connector of it that steers, and
that such a chassis carry legs: a leg on a base that rolls would hang from it, a
chassis with legs of its own walks on them alone, as its walking controller was
made for them, and a leg on a mount that steers, or on a part on that mount, would
turn about a kingpin no servo turns. A leg on a part fixed to the chassis, a
spacer, hangs as fixed as one on the chassis. A policy in a part's controller
was trained on the legs it walks, the part's own, so a chassis with no feet of
its own walks by a gait, or by a walker trained for it on its legs; a policy in
its own controller is refused.

### Walking controller

A `Legged` chassis may state the walking controller its legs walk by: a
policy, an ONNX file in the part's directory, that a page or a simulator calls
every so often with what it observes, and whose action sets the servos' targets;
or a gait, which needs no training ([below](#a-gait)), the one a chassis whose
legs are parts placed on it walks by. Without one the part loads and the
analysis and the rules judge it as they judge any; the `mjcf` target writes a
legged base only by its controller, or by a [walker](#walkers) trained for it.

```yaml
controller:
  policy: assets/policy.onnx     # an ONNX file in the part directory
  period: 0.02                   # s between two calls
  imu: {link: null, xyz: [-0.016, -0.067, -0.006], rpy: [0, 0, 0]}
  observation: [linear_velocity, angular_velocity, gravity, joint_angles,
                joint_velocities, last_action, command]
  action_scale: 0.5              # a servo's target: its hold plus this times the action
  simulator: {timestep: 0.004, integrator: Euler, iterations: 1, ls_iterations: 5,
              eulerdamp: false}
  basis: MuJoCo Playground's go1_policy.onnx (Apache-2.0)
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `policy` | yes | The policy, an ONNX file inside the part directory. The compiler copies it as it is and reads nothing of it |
| `period` | yes | The time between two calls (s), a whole number of the simulator's steps |
| `imu` | yes | Where the IMU is whose readings the policy observes: the `link` it is on, null for the part's frame, and its place `xyz` and turn `rpy` there |
| `observation` | yes | What the policy observes, each term once, in its order: `linear_velocity`, the IMU's linear velocity in its own frame; `angular_velocity`, its angular velocity; `gravity`, straight down, (0, 0, -1), in its frame, the transpose of its turn applied to it; `command`, ahead, to the left and turning left; `joint_angles`, each servo's angle from its `hold`, in the order of the part's links; `joint_velocities`, their speeds; `last_action`, the action it gave last; and `phase`, the gait's phase, the cosine of each foot's and then their sines |
| `hidden` | no | Links whose servos the policy reads as still: their angle and their speed read 0 |
| `action_scale` | yes | Each servo's target is its `hold` plus this times the action's term for it (positive) |
| `phase` | when `observation` lists `phase`, and only then | The gait's `frequency` (Hz) and each phase's offset, `offsets` (rad), at least one; with both `still_below` (positive) and `still_at`, each phase reads `still_at` while the command's length is under `still_below`, and goes on turning meanwhile |
| `simulator` | yes | The simulator the policy was trained in, as MuJoCo's `<option>` states it: `timestep` (s), `integrator` (`Euler`, `implicit` or `implicitfast`: not `RK4`, since the model is stepped in two halves, `mj_step1`, the controls, then `mj_step2`, which integrates by Euler under `RK4`), the solver's `iterations` and `ls_iterations` (whole, from 1 to 2147483647, the most MuJoCo reads), and `eulerdamp`, whether Euler's integrator damps the joints implicitly |
| `basis` | yes | Where the policy comes from |

The policy moves the chassis's servos, in the order of its links; the servos of
the parts mounted on it hold where they hold.

#### A gait

The walking controller may instead be a gait, which needs no training: a page or
a simulator works it out from the robot's own model as the robot walks. The legs,
taken in turn about the chassis's middle, step every other one half a period
apart. The feet on the floor carry the body level at its standing height and at
the speed it is told, and each foot in the air lands where that speed needs it.
The command it follows moves toward the one it is told by at most 1 m/s and
2 rad/s each second, so that told to stop at once from a run it slows over a
moment; it goes on stepping until the robot has settled, moving and turning
hardly at all at a period's workings of the gait in a row, and stops with
every foot down. [The output contract](output.md#the-mjcf-target) says how.

```yaml
controller:
  gait: {period: 0.4, duty: 0.55, step_height: 0.07}
  basis: a gait from the part's own model, with no training
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gait.period` | yes | The time a foot takes to step and stand again (s, positive) |
| `gait.duty` | yes | The part of the period each foot is on the floor: more than 0.5 and less than 1. Every foot is on the floor together for (duty - 0.5) times the period, twice a period, and the gait stops only then, once the robot has settled: at least 8 ms, two of the 4 ms the gait is worked out every. Each foot is in the air for (1 - duty) times the period, at least 40 ms, ten of them, to follow its arc |
| `gait.step_height` | yes | How high a foot is lifted (m, positive) |
| `basis` | yes | Where the gait's numbers come from |

A gait lifts every other leg, so the robot stands on an even number of feet,
four or more: a robot on two feet is balanced otherwise, which this version does
not do. Each foot steps by at least two servos between it and its part's frame,
one to lift it and one to swing it, and by servos of its own: a servo above two
feet, such as a spine's or a waist's, is not stepped by a gait in this version.
The loader asks this of a chassis's own legs, and
`kinematics.gait_walks_the_feet` of the robot's, the legs placed on it too. A leg
whose servos only pitch steps fore and aft alone, so the robot turns by the
strides of its sides, slowly; its `gait` states the turn it reaches. A gait
balances the model as it is, with the parts mounted on the chassis, and moves the
servos of the feet's legs; every other servo holds where it holds.

### Walkers

A robot assembled from a `Legged` body and legs that are parts of their own
walks by the gait its body states, which needs no training, or by a walker: a
policy trained for exactly that robot, which the library registers beside its
parts. A program whose `Legged` body and legs are a walker's walks by the
walker, whatever its body states, and takes the command the walker takes; the
`mjcf` target writes the walker's policy as the robot's drive. Its legs are the
walker's when each is the same part as one of the walker's, placed within a
millimetre of where the analysis places that one by its glue and turned within a
milliradian of how it turns it, each leg one of the walker's and each of the
walker's one leg, in whatever order the program declares them. Parts a program
mounts besides are carried, a load the policy was not trained with. Two walkers
of a library for the same robot are refused (`assembly.one_walker`): which one
the robot walks by is not the program's to say.

```yaml
# walkers/quad_walker/walker.yaml
schema_version: 1
id: quad_walker
description: the body on its four legs, walking by a policy trained for it
assembly:
  body: quad_body                  # a Legged chassis part without legs of its own
  limbs:                           # each leg on it, by a name of the walker's own
    fl: {part: hip_leg, glue: [0.12, 0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1]}
    fr: {part: hip_leg, glue: [0.12, -0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1]}
    rl: {part: hip_leg, glue: [-0.12, 0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1]}
    rr: {part: hip_leg, glue: [-0.12, -0.08, -0.04, 0, 0, -1]}
gait: {ahead: [-0.3, 0.6], aside: [-0.2, 0.2], turn: [-0.8, 0.8]}
controller:
  policy: assets/policy.onnx
  joints: [fl/hip, fl/knee, fr/hip, fr/knee, rl/hip, rl/knee, rr/hip, rr/knee]
  period: 0.02
  imu: {link: null, xyz: [0, 0, 0.02], rpy: [0, 0, 0]}
  observation: [linear_velocity, angular_velocity, gravity, command, joint_angles,
                joint_velocities, last_action]
  action_scale: 0.25
  simulator: {timestep: 0.004, integrator: Euler, iterations: 1, ls_iterations: 5,
              eulerdamp: false}
  basis: trained on the body on its four legs, in MuJoCo
provenance: {name: The body on its four legs, manufacturer: null, source_url: null, license: null}
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `assembly.body` | yes | The body the walker was trained with: a chassis part of the library with a `Legged` profile and no legs of its own |
| `assembly.limbs` | yes | Each leg placed on the body, by a name of the walker's own, any but `body`: its `part`, a leg of the library, and its `glue`, x, y and z, the unit normal nx, ny and nz and, when the program states one, the roll about it, as a program places it |
| `gait` | yes | The command the policy takes, its ranges as a `Legged` chassis states them |
| `controller` | yes | The policy, as a part's [walking controller](#walking-controller) states it, and `joints`: every servo of the body and its legs, each once, as `owner/link`, the owner `body` or a limb's name, in the order the policy reads and moves them. `hidden` names servos as `joints` does, and the IMU's `link` is one of the body's links, or null for its frame |
| `provenance` | yes | Where the walker comes from, as a part's |

A walker that does not state a robot of the library's parts, whose file gives a
key twice, whose policy does not move every servo of it or has none to move, or
that places two legs of one part by glues within twice that millimetre and
milliradian of each other, where a leg placed between them would be either, is a
diagnostic, and the robot does not walk by it; the parts still load.

### Objects

An entry of category `object` is a thing a world places, a table, a shelf, a
ramp, and not a part of a robot. A `.world` entity names it by `ref`. It
states what is shown of it and what of it collides:

```yaml
schema_version: 1
id: ramp_10deg                       # equals the directory name
category: object
description: A ramp 0.8 m wide that rises 10 degrees along +x over one metre, from the floor at its frame.

visual:                              # the mesh that is shown
  file: assets/model.glb
  xyz: [0, 0, 0]
  rpy: [0, 0, 0]

collision:                           # the shapes it collides by; absent when it is only shown
  - type: box                        # box | sphere | cylinder
    size: [1.01543, 0.8, 0.05]       # a slab, tilted so that its top face is the ramp's surface
    origin_xyz: [0.50434, 0, 0.06354]
    rpy: [0, -0.174533, 0]

provenance:
  name: null
  manufacturer: null
  source_url: null
  license: null
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version`, `id`, `category`, `description` | yes | As for a part; `category` is `object` |
| `visual` | yes | As for a part: the mesh a simulator shows, with where it sits in the object's frame |
| `collision` | no | A list of at least one shape. Each states `type` (`box`, `sphere` or `cylinder`), `size` (three positive numbers: a box's sides; a sphere's diameter and a cylinder's in `x`, a cylinder's height in `z`, as a world entity's `size` reads), `origin_xyz` and `rpy`, its place and its fixed-axis roll, pitch and yaw in the object's frame. The targets collide the object by these shapes, the navigation map is drawn from them and a run is judged against them, each shape projected onto the ground where the entity stands. Without `collision` the object is only shown, and no entity that collides can be made of it |
| `provenance` | no | As for a part, without a price: an object is not bought. Of an object whose mesh is a model someone else published, `name` is the model, `manufacturer` its author, `source_url` where it lies and `license` the licence it is passed on under |

An object collides by shapes and never by its mesh. The compiler opens no
mesh, so it could neither draw one onto the map nor judge a run against it,
and the two simulators would not agree on it: MuJoCo collides a mesh by its
convex hull, which fills the space under a table, and reads no glTF.

Both simulators take a mesh's coordinates as they are, in metres with z up,
after the transforms of the file's nodes; neither turns a glTF from its y-up
convention. Gazebo decodes the mesh. MuJoCo decodes no glTF, so the
`ros-mujoco-nav2` target's node reads it: a `.glb`, or a `.gltf` with its
buffers beside it or written into it, as every triangle of the file's default
scene in its material's base colour (`baseColorFactor`) with the picture laid
on it (`baseColorTexture`), without the material's other maps, the light it
states it gives off (`emissiveFactor`), normals or vertex colours. It does not read a mesh that requires an extension (a
compressed or quantized mesh), a sparse accessor, anything drawn as points,
lines, strips or fans, a picture that is not a PNG, which is all MuJoCo
decodes, or one moved or scaled where it is laid (`KHR_texture_transform`):
the node stops as it starts and says which stands in the way. Of an object whose mesh is not glTF that target shows the
shapes the object collides by, and it refuses one that only shows
(`target.unsupported`), of which nothing would be in the scene.

An object states none of `inertial`, `connectors`, `profiles`, `wheel`,
`track`, `range`, `motor`, `battery`, `driver` and `contacts`; each is
`library.unsupported` on it. A world holds an object where the program places
it, so it states no mass; nothing mates onto it, so it states no connectors;
and whether the robot may touch it is the entity type's to say in the world
that places it, so it states no profiles.

### Environments

An entry of category `environment` is a place a `.world` scenario takes whole
by `ref`: a room, a hall with its shelves. It has no mesh and no shape of its
own; it states its floor and the entities that stand in it.

```yaml
schema_version: 1
id: room_6x4                         # equals the directory name; never `empty`
category: environment
description: A storeroom 6 m by 4 m with walls 0.5 m high, a work table in a corner and a mark on the floor where a robot docks.

ground_plane: true                   # whether it brings its floor

entities:                            # name -> what a .world entity states
  wall_north: {entity: Obstacle, type: box, size: [6.2, 0.1, 0.5], pos: [2, 2.05, 0.25, 0, 0, 0, 1]}
  table: {entity: Obstacle, ref: work_table, pos: [4.5, 1.1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1]}
  dock: {entity: Marker, ref: floor_disc, pos: [4.0, -1.0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1]}
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version`, `id`, `category`, `description` | yes | As for a part; `category` is `environment`. The id may not be `empty`, which a scenario writes for no environment |
| `ground_plane` | yes | `true` or `false`: whether the environment brings its floor, which is the world's one ground plane. No scenario of a world that takes such an environment may add `ground_plane = true`; two environments that each bring a floor share the one |
| `entities` | yes | A mapping, which may be empty, from an entity's name (an identifier) to its fields, below |
| `provenance` | no | As for a part |

An entity's fields are the [parameters of a `.world` entity](vocabulary.md#entity-types),
by their names and in their forms, so that the lines of a scenario move into a
library unchanged in meaning:

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `entity` | yes | The entity type: `Obstacle`, `SupportSurface` or `Marker`. The vocabulary's, so it is resolved when a program takes the environment |
| `type` | one of `type` and `ref` | A primitive: `box`, `sphere` or `cylinder` |
| `size` | with `type`; not with `ref` | `[x, y, z]`, positive, as a `.world` entity's |
| `ref` | one of `type` and `ref` | The id of a library [object](#objects). It may be another library's that the program is compiled with, so it is resolved when a program takes the environment |
| `pos` | yes | `[x, y, z, qx, qy, qz, qw]` in the world's frame; the quaternion of unit length |
| `collision` | no | `true` or `false`; without it the entity type decides, as in a `.world` file |

An environment's entities are static, like every entity, and state no
`is_static`. A scenario takes them where they stand: it gives the environment
no pose. Once taken they are the scenario's own entities, in the world's one
namespace beside the program's.

### Bus names

A bus name is the library's own: the compiler only compares a motor's `bus`
with the `buses` of the driver that commands it. Name the wire and the
protocol together (`dynamixel_ttl`, `dynamixel_rs485`), since two makers'
servos on the same wire do not answer each other's boards.

### Profiles

A profile is one component type the part can be used as, named exactly as the
vocabulary names the type, and maps the logical mount names of that type to
the part's connectors. The `Mecanum_four_wheel` profile of a frame maps
`front_left_wheel`, ..., and `middle_top`; a wheel's or a sensor's profile
maps `default`, the connector the part mates by, and so do a battery's and a
motor driver's; a track's maps `default`, the hub that drives it, whose
connector carries no joint, since the unit does not turn about its hub; a motor's maps `default`, the
face it seats on a chassis' drive mount by, and `shaft`, the end of its output
shaft, where a wheel mates. The shaft connector carries no joint: the wheel's
connector carries the `continuous` joint, so the joint is between motor and
wheel. Two logical mounts may not share a connector. Which types exist and
which mounts each needs is vocabulary, decided by the semantic phase, not by
this format.

A profile maps mounts and nothing else. Which mounts of a chassis type steer
is vocabulary; which of them are driven is what the program places, a motor on
the mount or on a seat whose driveline turns it, within what the type allows.

## Diagnostics

Every problem is a diagnostic in the `library_load` phase that points into
the file. A problem with `library.yaml` itself blocks: nothing can be loaded.
A part with any problem in its declaration is left out of the loaded library,
so later phases never see a half-checked record, and the diagnostic is a
warning that does not block a program which never names the part; a program
that names such a part gets a name-resolution error that repeats why the part
could not be loaded. A shared catalog with a few incomplete declarations thus
still serves every program that uses its complete parts.

| Code | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `library.manifest_missing` | No `library.yaml` at the given root (an environment failure: there is nothing to point at) |
| `library.yaml_syntax` | The file is not valid YAML, or no tree that can be read: an alias inside the value its anchor names, values nested more than 64 levels deep, or aliases that expand it to more than 200,000 values. An alias otherwise stands for a copy of the value its anchor names |
| `library.duplicate_key` | A key given twice; both occurrences are shown |
| `library.invalid_key` | A key that is not a plain name |
| `library.unknown_field` | A key the schema does not list; the message lists the allowed ones |
| `library.missing_field` | A required key is absent, or a link that turns on a revolute joint has no `servo`, or a wheel has no `wheel` block, or a part with a `Range` profile no `range` block, or one with a `Motor` profile no `motor` block or no `shaft` mount, or one with a `Battery` profile no `battery` block, or one with a `Track` profile no `track` block, or one with a `MotorDriver` profile no `driver` block, neither `channels` nor `buses` in it, or `channels` without their supply range and continuous current, or a part states one end of a voltage range without the other, or an estimate has no `basis`, or a chassis used as `Legged` states no `gait`, or `feet` without `links`, or a leg states no `links` or no `feet`, or a foot no `link`, `shape` or `friction`, or a gait no `ahead`, `aside` or `turn`, or a controller states neither a `policy` nor a `gait`, or a policy no `period`, `imu`, `observation`, `action_scale`, `simulator` or `basis`, or no `phase` while its observation lists the phase, or its phase one of `still_below` and `still_at` without the other, or a gait no `period`, `duty` or `step_height`, or no `basis` |
| `library.wrong_type` | A value of the wrong shape: not a mapping, not a number, not `[x, y, z]`, an object's or a link's `collision` that is not a list of shapes or is an empty one, `links` that name no link, a link joint's `range` that is not two numbers, `feet` that name no foot or a foot that is not a mapping, a foot's `link` that is not a name or its `shape` or `friction` not a number, a gait's range that is not two numbers, a controller's `observation` that names no term, a phase's `offsets` that give none, a simulator's `eulerdamp` that is not true or false, ... |
| `library.invalid_value` | A value of the right shape but impossible: a number other than 0 nearer zero than 1e-100 or larger than 1e30, zero mass, a negative radius, an inertia tensor that is not positive definite or whose principal moments violate the triangle inequality by more than the rounding of its decimals, an unknown category, an unknown joint type, a driveline that names a connector twice or turns a motor's seat, a track whose run on the ground has no length, a `visual.file` that lies beside the declaration and not in a directory of its own, a shape of an object's collision that is none of `box`, `sphere` and `cylinder`, an environment named `empty` or one of its entities with both or neither of `type` and `ref`, a path that escapes the part directory or is not written plainly with `/` (`./`, a backslash, an empty segment), a file that does, or a file beside a mesh, that links out of the part directory, a hull with fewer than four corners, a face that is not a triangle or names a corner the hull does not have, a hull that is not convex, a hull whose triangles leave an edge open, put a third triangle on an edge, repeat a triangle or a corner of one, or enclose no volume, a link's name that is not an identifier, a link's `parent` that is no link declared above it, a link joint that is neither `revolute` nor `fixed` or whose `range` does not run from a lower angle to a higher one, a link's shape that is none of `box`, `sphere`, `cylinder` and `capsule`, a servo's `kp` or `effort` that is not positive, its `damping`, `armature` or `frictionloss` negative, or its `hold` outside its joint's range, a part used as `Legged` that is not a chassis, a foot's name that is not an identifier, a foot on a link the part does not have or on a shape its link does not have (counted from 0, a whole number), two feet on one shape, a foot's `friction` that is not positive, a gait's range that runs from a higher speed to a lower one or leaves out standing still, a controller's `period` that is no whole number of its simulator's steps, an observation term that is none of the eight or is named twice, a `hidden` link that no servo turns or that is named twice, an IMU on a link the part does not have, a `phase` its observation does not list, a policy on a part none of whose links has a servo, an integrator other than `Euler`, `implicit` and `implicitfast`, iterations that are not whole numbers from 1 to 2147483647, or a `period`, an `action_scale`, a `frequency`, a `still_below` or a `timestep` that is not positive |
| `library.not_unit_vector` | A `dir`, `up`, or joint `axis`, a link joint's among them, that is not unit length (tolerance 0.001), or the quaternion of an environment entity's `pos` |
| `library.unsupported` | A field that exists but is not valid for this part: `collision` on a wheel, `wheel` on a sensor, `range` on a part that is not a range finder, `motor` on a part that is not a motor, `battery` on a part that is not a battery, `driver` on a part that is not a motor driver, `track` on a part that is not a track, a joint on a track's connector, a channel's current on a driver without `channels`, `steering` or `driveline` outside a chassis, an `axis` on a fixed joint, a box's `size` or `origin_xyz` on a hull, a hull's `vertices` or `faces` on a box, a part's field (`inertial`, `connectors`, `profiles`, ...) on an object or an environment, `size` beside an environment entity's `ref`, `links` on a part that is not a chassis, an attachment or a leg, an `axis` or a `range` on a fixed link joint, a `servo` on a fixed one, `feet` on a part that is neither used as `Legged` nor a leg, a `gait` or a `controller` on a part whose profiles do not list `Legged` or on a leg, a controller that is a policy on a chassis with no feet of its own, a foot on a cylinder |
| `library.asset_missing` | `visual.file` or a controller's `policy` names a file that does not exist |
| `library.id_mismatch` | `id` differs from the directory name |
| `library.unknown_connector` | A mount names a connector the part does not declare, or a driveline does |
| `library.duplicate_part`, `library.part_missing` | A part registered twice, or registered without a declaration |

## Not in this version

These are needed and not yet accepted; a declaration that contains them is
rejected rather than silently ignored: a field for them with
`library.unknown_field`, a link joint that slides or a link whose parent is
declared after it with `library.invalid_value`.

- A connector on one of a part's links (a camera on a pan-tilt's head): a
  part's connectors are in its own frame. A link joint that slides, and links
  that close a loop, such as a leg moved through a linkage.
- Shared interface types (`interfaces/`) that make two connectors compatible
  by declaration rather than by name.
- The frame of a sensor part follows REP 103: it looks along its own +x axis,
  so a mount whose `up` is the chassis' +x makes a camera look forward.
- Sensor specifications (field of view, range, rate, noise), except a range
  finder's `range` block, and a steering actuator's limits. The target still
  fills these in from its own defaults.
- Two motors on one driveline that are geared to each other, a driveline's
  losses, and how a differential shares torque when it is locked.
- A track on a steered mount, flippers, and a belt's own links and tension.
- Source tags on values other than the inertial.
- Assemblies: a part made of other parts, such as a kit, that a program places as one.
  A walker names the parts it was trained with, which a program places one by one.
- An object that moves, is pushed or opens, an object's scale, and an object
  that collides by its mesh.
- An environment placed at a pose or taken twice, one built of other
  environments, and goals or regions an environment names beside its entities.

## Changes from the previous compiler's `part.yaml`

The facts are the same; the file moved and a few names changed. A converter
belongs to the library repository.

| Was | Is | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<category>/<id>/part.yaml`, JSON text | `parts/<id>/component.yaml`, YAML | the library repository's layout; `category` is a field |
| `model` | `visual` | it is the visual model; collision and inertial are separate |
| `geometry: {radius, height}` | `wheel: {radius, width}` | says what it is |
| top-level `joint` | `connectors.<name>.joint` | the joint belongs to the mating point that creates it |
| `pos_local`, `dir_local`, `up_local` | `pos`, `dir`, `up` | every vector is in the part frame; the suffix said nothing |
| `estimate_basis` | `basis` | |
| `images`, `catalog` | not read | presentation and catalog data; the compiler no longer fails a compile because a preview image is missing |


## From the previous format

The component library repository declared its parts for the previous compiler
as `<category>/<id>/part.yaml` (`schema_version: 3`). `tools/convert-library
SOURCE DESTINATION` writes such a checkout in this format: `model` becomes
`visual` with the mesh copied under `assets/`, `pos_local`, `dir_local` and
`up_local` lose their suffix, a wheel's `geometry` becomes `wheel` (its
`height` is the `width`), the part's `joint` moves onto its connector, and
`estimate_basis` becomes `basis`. Each profile is renamed to the component
type it is (`laser` to `Lidar`, `diff_four_wheel` to `Diff_drive`, the
`arm`, `battery` and `circuit` kinds to `Attachment`), and what the compiler
never reads (`images`, `catalog`) is dropped. The converter invents nothing:
a placeholder inertial without a basis, or a steered mount whose connector
declares no kingpin, stays as it was and the loader reports it on the result.
The report of the conversion names every value it dropped or could not carry.

# Validation rules

This page is generated from `mobiledsl.validation.standard`; edit the code, not
the page. Each rule asks one question of the facts analysis derived and answers
`pass`, `fail`, `unknown` or `not_applicable` with the evidence it used. `fail`
is an error that blocks compilation, except for an advisory rule, whose `fail` is
a warning: the facts show a likely mistake that a program may still mean.
`unknown` means the facts do not settle the question, usually because a library
part did not state something; it is never a pass: each place it points at is a
warning, and the compile's summary counts the rule as undecided. A rule answers for
each place it points at: one that fails for one part and cannot decide another
says both, the second as a warning. A rule reads facts; it does not recompute
geometry and does not change the program.

| Rule | Category | Question | `fail` is | `unknown` when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `assembly.glue_on_connector` | assembly | Does every component's glue name one connector of the chassis or of a part placed on it, and is that part placed? | an error | never |
| `assembly.one_part_per_connector` | assembly | Does each chassis connector carry at most one part? | an error | never |
| `assembly.wheel_mounts_filled` | assembly | Does every drive mount of the chassis type carry one wheel or track, on the mount or on the shaft of a motor on it, with any motor that turns it on the mount or on a seat of the chassis whose driveline turns it; does every other wheel mount carry one free wheel; and does nothing that drives sit elsewhere? | an error | never |
| `assembly.wheel_type_matches_chassis` | assembly | Is every wheel that rolls, and every track, of a type the chassis takes? | an error | never |
| `assembly.steering_declared` | assembly | Does each steered mount of the chassis type carry an upright kingpin? | an error | never |
| `kinematics.omni_wheels_span_the_plane` | kinematics | Do an omni base's rolling directions span the plane? | an error | when no omni wheel is placed |
| `assembly.axles_horizontal` | assembly | Is the axle of every wheel that rolls, and of every track's hub, horizontal? | an error | never |
| `assembly.wheels_touch_one_plane` | assembly | Do all wheels, and both ends of every track's run, touch the ground on one plane, with each other and with a legged robot's feet (within 2 mm)? | an error | never |
| `assembly.feet_touch_the_ground` | assembly | Does every foot of a legged robot, of its chassis's own legs or of a leg placed on it, touch the ground on one plane with the others (within 2 mm), where the servos hold the legs? | an error | never |
| `assembly.legs_on_a_legged_chassis` | assembly | Is every leg placed on a Legged chassis that has no legs of its own, hanging from no connector of it that steers, and does such a chassis carry legs? | an error | never |
| `assembly.one_walker` | assembly | Is the robot, its body and its legs placed as they are, the robot of one walker of its chassis's library at most? | an error | never |
| `assembly.links_clear_the_ground` | assembly | Does every shape of a part's links but a legged robot's feet stay above the ground (within 2 mm), where its servos hold the links? | an error | no wheel, track or foot is placed |
| `statics.mass_inside_the_wheel_contacts` | statics | Does the robot's centre of mass fall strictly inside the polygon of its ground contacts, the wheels, the tracks' runs, a legged robot's feet and the skids its parts declare, counting a skid a little above the wheels' plane once the base has tipped onto it, with no skid reaching below the wheels or the feet? | an error | no wheel, track or foot is placed, a wheel, a track's end or a foot is off the plane the others share, or the contacts lie on one line and the robot tips onto nothing declared |
| `assembly.footprint_known` | assembly | Do the parts' collision shapes, their links' with them where their servos hold them, bound the robot's footprint? | an error | a placed part declares no collision box |
| `assembly.parts_clear_each_other` | assembly | Do the declared shapes of the parts fixed to the base, each part's links' with it where their servos hold them, keep out of each other, but for what a well on a connector of either lets into that part's declared shape? | a warning | no two shapes are found to overlap, and a placed part declares no collision shape |
| `assembly.wheels_clear_other_parts` | assembly | Does every other part's declared shape, its links' with it where their servos hold them, keep out of the space each wheel turns through, over its steering lock, and out of each track's unit, but for what a well on the part's connector lets into its declared shape? | an error | no part is found in a wheel's or a track's way, and a placed part or a track's unit declares no collision box or a stretch of a steering lock could not be settled within the analysis's budget |
| `kinematics.spin_supported` | kinematics | If the task spins in place, can the base, and a walking base the way its gait turns? | an error | never |
| `kinematics.strafe_supported` | kinematics | If the task strafes, is the base holonomic, and does a walking base's gait move aside to that side, as fast as the task states? | an error | never |
| `kinematics.walk_supported` | kinematics | If the task advances, backs up or navigates a walking base, does its gait walk that way, as fast as the task states, and turn either way to navigate? | an error | never |
| `kinematics.gait_walks_the_feet` | kinematics | If the chassis walks by a gait, does the robot stand on an even number of feet, four or more, each stepping by at least two servos of its own? | an error | never |
| `kinematics.tracks_state_their_travel` | kinematics | Does every track's part state how far its belt travels per turn of its hub? | an error | a track's part states no travel per turn |
| `sensing.range_clears_the_ground` | sensing | Does every Range sensor's cone stay above the ground within its range? | a warning | no wheel, track or foot is placed |
| `power.supply_voltage_accepted` | power | Is the voltage every motor and motor driver is fed, full and run down, within the range its part states it accepts? | an error | a part that states a range names no supply, or its battery states a nominal voltage within that range and no range of its own |
| `power.rated_voltage_in_supply` | power | Does the voltage every motor is fed, between full and run down, include the voltage its ratings hold at? | a warning | a motor names no supply, or its battery states only a nominal voltage that is not the motor's rated one |
| `power.driver_delivers_stall_current` | power | Can every motor driver deliver, from one channel, the current the motor on it draws stalled? | a warning | never |
| `command.driver_commands_its_motors` | command | Does every motor's driver have what commands it: a channel of its own for a motor without a bus, the motor's bus for one that carries its driver? | an error | a motor names no driver |
| `command.driver_has_a_channel_for_each_motor` | command | Does every motor driver have a channel of its own for each motor it drives? | a warning | never |

# Diagnostics

Every phase reports problems through one diagnostic type, defined in
`src/mobiledsl/support/diagnostics.py`. A diagnostic points at the source
bytes that caused it, says what to change, and states the facts the decision
rests on. The same object renders as a terminal line and as JSON.

## The diagnostic

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `code` | Stable identifier: two or more dotted `lower_snake_case` segments, for example `syntax.unexpected_token`, `name.duplicate`. Codes never change meaning; a changed check gets a new code. |
| `message` | One sentence naming the cause. |
| `level` | Presentation only: `error`, `warning`, `note`, `help`. |
| `phase` | The compiler phase that produced it (below). |
| `failure_domain` | Who owns the failure: `application` (the program or a library), `invocation` (command-line arguments), `environment` (files the compiler cannot read or write). |
| `base_disposition`, `effective_disposition` | Whether it blocks compilation: `blocking` or `non_blocking`. The base value is the check's own judgement; the effective value may be changed by invocation policy, and then `disposition_reason` says why. |
| `primary` | The span that caused the diagnostic, with a short label. |
| `related` | Other spans that explain it, each with a label, for example the first declaration of a duplicate name. |
| `edits` | Machine-applicable replacements, if the fix is certain. |
| `help` | What the reader should change. One short line per entry. |
| `notes` | The facts the decision rests on. One short line per entry. |

Level and blocking are independent. An `error` is normally blocking and a
`warning` normally not, but `--warnings-as-errors` changes the effective
disposition of a warning without changing its level, and the reason is
recorded on the diagnostic.

### Phases

In execution order: `source_load`, `library_load`, `target_resolution`,
`parse`, `name_resolution`, `type_check`, `analysis`, `validation`,
`target_binding`, `world_realization`, `emission`, `output_write`. Each phase
ends in one status: `pass`, `invalid`, `environment_failed`, `not_run`, or
`not_requested`.

### Codes

| Code | Phase | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `invocation.unknown_source_kind`, `invocation.duplicate_source_kind`, `invocation.source_missing` | source_load | a file that is not `.core`, `.world`, `.task` or `.eval`, two files of one form, or a required form not given |
| `invocation.unknown_target`, `invocation.no_target`, `invocation.no_output`, `invocation.output_overlaps_input` | source_load | a `--target` that does not exist, `--output` without `--target` or the reverse, or an output directory that is, holds, or sits inside an input |
| `environment.source_unreadable` | source_load | a source file the compiler cannot read |
| `syntax.unexpected_token` | parse | a token no rule allows here; the message says what was expected, in plain words |
| `syntax.unexpected_character` | parse | a character that starts no token, for example `#` |
| `syntax.unexpected_eof` | parse | the source ends inside a declaration |
| `syntax.invalid` | parse | any other parser failure |
| `syntax.unknown_reference_namespace` | parse | a reference whose namespace is not `core`, `world`, or `task`; the declaration is still built |
| `syntax.number_out_of_range` | parse | a number too large for a 64-bit float, such as `1e999` |
| `syntax.duplicate_parameter` | parse | a parameter given twice in one argument list; the primary is the second occurrence and the first is related |
| `library.*` | library_load | problems in a component library; listed in [Component library format](library.md#diagnostics) |
| `name.unknown_component_type`, `name.unknown_entity_type`, `name.unknown_node_type`, `name.unknown_check` | name_resolution | a type name the vocabulary does not have; `help` suggests a near miss |
| `name.unknown_part`, `name.ambiguous_part`, `name.part_category_mismatch`, `name.type_not_supported` | name_resolution | the `ref` of a component names no part, several parts, a part of another category, an object or an environment, or a part without the type's profile |
| `name.unknown_object`, `name.ambiguous_object`, `name.not_an_object` | name_resolution | the `ref` of a world entity names no object or one that could not be loaded, an object several libraries have, or a part of a robot or an environment |
| `name.unknown_environment`, `name.ambiguous_environment`, `name.not_an_environment` | name_resolution | the `ref` of a scenario names no environment or one that could not be loaded, an environment several libraries have, or a part or an object. A world name the program does not declare is not reported beside it: it may be the missing environment's |
| `name.unknown_reference` | name_resolution | an `@core/`, `@world/` or `@task/` reference that nothing declares |
| `name.duplicate` | name_resolution | two components, entities or goals with one name, or `physics`/`spawn` given twice |
| `name.chassis_missing`, `name.multiple_chassis` | name_resolution | a robot needs exactly one chassis |
| `type.unknown_parameter`, `type.missing_parameter` | type_check | an argument the type does not take, or a required one that is absent |
| `type.wrong_value_type`, `type.wrong_tuple_length`, `type.invalid_choice`, `type.not_positive`, `type.not_unit_vector`, `type.not_unit_quaternion` | type_check | an argument of the wrong shape or an impossible value |
| `type.wrong_reference` | type_check | a reference to the wrong namespace or kind, for example `Navigate(goal = @core/...)` |
| `type.exactly_one_of` | type_check | an entity needs one of `type`/`ref`; a goal one of `pose`/`target` |
| `type.size_needs_type` | type_check | an entity states `size` beside `ref`; an object has the size its library entry states |
| `type.second_ground_plane` | type_check | a scenario states `ground_plane = true` in a world that already has its floor: an environment of any of its scenarios brings one, or another scenario lays it |
| `type.object_without_collision` | type_check | an entity that collides, an `Obstacle`, a `SupportSurface` or one with `collision = true`, is made of an object that declares no collision |
| `type.children_required`, `type.children_not_allowed`, `type.one_child_required` | type_check | a composite without a child node or a task without a node, a block under an action, or a decorator without exactly one child |
| `type.bound_required`, `type.bounds_inverted` | type_check | a check without `min` or `max`, or with `min` above `max` |
| `validation.<rule>` | validation | a rule that failed (an error, or a warning for an advisory rule) or could not decide (a warning); the rules are listed in [Validation rules](validation.md) |
| `target.unsupported` | target_binding | a construct the chosen target cannot realize; [Target output](output.md) lists them |
| `target.blind_navigation` | target_binding | a warning: the task navigates, but the robot has no range sensor to feed the costmaps |
| `environment.output_unwritable` | output_write | the output directory cannot be written |
| `environment.output_linked` | output_write | a directory inside the output is a symbolic link, which the compiler does not write through |

The parser stops at the first syntax error, so a source with several syntax
errors reports one per compile. Every later phase runs over the whole input
and reports every occurrence, so one compile shows everything it can.

## Locations

A span is a half-open range of UTF-8 bytes in one source, identified by the
name the compiler was given for that source, usually its path. Spans are
exact: a diagnostic about a name covers exactly the bytes of that name.

For people, a byte offset is shown as a one-based line and a one-based
column counted in Unicode scalar values. Line terminators may be LF or CRLF.
JSON output carries both the byte offset and the line and column.

## Terminal form

The terminal form follows rustc and ruff, so a reader who knows those tools
needs no new convention:

```text
<level>[<code>]: <message>
  --> <source>:<line>:<column>
  |
N | <source line>
  |       ------ <related label>
...
M | <source line>
  |       ^^^^^^ <primary label>
  |
  = help: <what to change>
  = help: <edit message> at <source>:<line>:<column>: '<replacement>'
  = note: <fact>
  = note: <related label> at <other source>:<line>:<column>
```

The heading names the level, the code, and the cause. The arrow gives the
primary location. The excerpt shows every source line that carries a span:
the primary span is underlined with carets, related spans in the same source
with dashes, and lines with nothing to show are elided as `...`. A span that
continues onto later lines is underlined to the end of its first line; an
empty span, such as the insertion point for a missing declaration, gets one
caret. Tabs are shown as four spaces. The footer lists `help` (from `help`
and from machine edits) and `note` (from `notes`, from related spans in other
sources, from related spans beyond the first three as `and N more`, and the
reason when the effective disposition differs from the base). A span whose
source is not loaded is shown as `<source>:bytes <start>..<end>` with no
excerpt.

Color is applied when the output is a terminal. `NO_COLOR` disables it,
`FORCE_COLOR` enables it for a pipe, and `TERM=dumb` disables it; this is the
order those variables have in other CLIs. The level and the primary
underline use the level's color (`error` red, `warning` yellow, `note` cyan,
`help` green), the message is bold, and the gutter, arrows, and related
underlines are blue. Color never changes the text.

Example, a duplicate name:

```text
error[name.duplicate]: component 'wheel_lf' is declared twice
   --> demo.core:18:13
   |
17 |     Mecanum wheel_lf(ref = "mecanum_black", glue = (0.1275, 0.1494, -0.0216, 0, 1, 0))
   |             -------- first declared here
18 |     Mecanum wheel_lf(ref = "mecanum_black", glue = (-0.1275, 0.1494, -0.0216, 0, 1, 0))
   |             ^^^^^^^^ declared again here
   |
```

Example, a syntax error:

```text
error[syntax.unexpected_token]: unexpected 'glue'; expected one of ')', ','
   --> demo.core:22:40
   |
22 |     Lidar top_lidar(ref = "lidar_ld06" glue = (0, 0.0001, 0.0344, 0, 0, -1))
   |                                        ^^^^ not allowed here
   |
```

## JSON form

```json
{
  "code": "name.duplicate",
  "level": "error",
  "message": "component 'wheel_lf' is declared twice",
  "phase": "name_resolution",
  "failure_domain": "application",
  "disposition": {"base": "blocking", "effective": "blocking"},
  "primary": {
    "span": {
      "source": "demo.core",
      "start": {"byte_offset": 1163, "line": 18, "column": 13},
      "end": {"byte_offset": 1171, "line": 18, "column": 21}
    },
    "label": "declared again here"
  },
  "related": [
    {
      "span": {
        "source": "demo.core",
        "start": {"byte_offset": 1076, "line": 17, "column": 13},
        "end": {"byte_offset": 1084, "line": 17, "column": 21}
      },
      "label": "first declared here"
    }
  ]
}
```

This is the same diagnostic as the terminal example above.

Keys that would be empty (`related`, `edits`, `help`, `notes`) are omitted.
`disposition.reason` is present only when the effective disposition differs
from the base. An edit has `applicability` (only `machine_applicable`
exists), a `span`, a `replacement`, and an optional `message`.

## Ordering

A stream of diagnostics is sorted before it is shown or serialized, so the
output does not depend on traversal order. The key is: phase order, then
primary span (source name, start byte, end byte, label), then level, code,
message, failure domain, dispositions, then the related spans and edits.

## Machine edits

An edit replaces one span with UTF-8 text. Edits within one source must not
overlap and must not share a start offset. Applying them never mutates the
loaded sources; the result is new bytes per source. Only edits whose
correctness is certain are attached; a suggestion the author has to judge is
`help` text.

## Rules for writing a diagnostic

- Point at the bytes that caused the problem, in the program or in the part
  file. A diagnostic with no span is a last resort for environment failures.
- Name the cause in the message. Put what to change in `help` and the facts
  in `notes`; do not mix them.
- Never resolve an ambiguity for the author. Report every candidate as
  related and produce no result.
- A missing value is `unknown`, never a default; say which value is missing
  and where it is declared.
- The code is part of the interface: tests and repair tools match on it.
